A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in isolated regions.  This study examines the presence of massive stars in the less crowded surroundings of the relatively young Westerlund 2 cluster to shed light on this issue.  Spectral types of O stars in Westerlund 2 have been determined, and by comparing their colors to theoretical models, we estimated the masses and ages of these stars.  We found that most of these stars are approximately 1 million years old and have masses greater than 30 times that of the sun, consistent with cluster estimates.  Although some stars appear to be out of order along the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, this can be explained by small uncertainties in mass estimates and early strong mass loss.  This study confirms that massive star formation can occur in dense clusters and less crowded surroundings equally, suggesting a wide range of possible environments for this type of star formation.  Additionally, we found no evidence of mass overspread in Westerlund 2, and masses of all stars show a relatively uniform distribution around a certain value.  This might be the result of dynamic processes in the cluster that prevent massive star propagation.  Further research is needed to observe these stars repeatedly to make definitive conclusions regarding their movements.  We suggest that metal-rich environments that are not too dense from the start may lead to widespread star formation in all directions.  Clusters that are dense from the start may experience rapid and uniform star formation first in the dense core.  This theory is similar to the galactic fountain theory that describes similar patterns in star formation.  Furthermore, we found 6 O stars without counterparts in the cluster catalog, which might be missing an entry or could be extragalactic objects.  Moreover, we identified 4 O stars with proposed masses and ages that are inconsistent with cluster estimates, suggesting that further investigation using other methods, such as Gaia data, is needed to confirm their status as cluster members.  Additionally, we found 3 O stars with proposed ages approximately 1 million years that are likely to be extragalactic objects or 3 times as old as the cluster. In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. In response, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. However, these approaches either underutilize the temporal information available or propose test vehicles that may not support real-world applications. To address these limitations, this paper introduces an innovative deep learning-based channel estimation scheme for IEEE 802.11p. This estimator leverages temporal averaging and bidirectional training to enhance deep learning-based channel estimation performance. In our experiments, this new scheme demonstrated superior performance across various scenarios. Additionally, we observed that our estimator did not introduce additional test vehicle complexity. Finally, we found that our scheme outperformed the standard IEEE 802.11p by 30%. Furthermore, our results showed that our scheme performed 10% better than a recent, state-of-the-art deep learning-based estimator. In summary, our approach is a straightforward integration of temporal averaging and bidirectional training into a deep learning-based IEEE 802.11p estimator. This effort addresses a critical challenge in vehicular communications and serves as a model for utilizing bidirectional training in deep learning applications. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We experiment with employing various models in the RGB and L*a*b color spaces, relying on transfer learning and pre-trained ResNet-18 architecture, due to the small size of the dataset available. Our approach successfully produces aesthetically pleasing, high-resolution, and colorized results for images lacking these characteristics. The performance of the proposed model is quantitatively assessed by measuring distance metrics, including L1 distance and L2 distance, and evaluating the generated images against the real data distribution using the Frechet inception distance (FID) metric. Additionally, the effectiveness of the model is subject to qualitative assessment by astronomers. The proposed colorization approach surpasses human expectations, achieving improvements of approximately 30% in the FID metric over various distance metrics. The code used to generate and display the results is publicly accessible on GitHub, enabling reproduction of the findings. The dataset employed in this research is also publicly available, labeled 'Astronomical Colorization', under the following link https://www.ikz.uni-koeln.de/datasets/ikz_astronomical_colorization. pdf. The generated images can be viewed on our website at https://ikz.uni-koeln.de/projects/ikz_astronomical_colorization. Furthermore, the generated images and dataset are also hosted on Unsplash and Datashare for global access. We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of partial differential equations. The approach works by determining the weights for each neuron in localized data subsets where a corresponding approximation matrix remains invertible, thereby rendering hyperparameter optimization unnecessary. As a direct consequence, this minimizes computational speed. With inherent overfitting prevention, our method provides reproducible results that are also easily interpretable. With respect to observations and features, our method's computational complexity lies in the P class and has a specific running time expressed in terms of these variables. Conversely, traditional ANN training algorithms fall into the NP-Complete class. Its exceptional generalization capability allows the method to achieve test-set errors comparable to or even lower than those on the training data. This is evident from the outstanding performance shown by the method in numerous experiments, including its successful 98.2% accuracy in classifying the MNIST dataset for handwritten digits, and its achievement of marginally higher accuracy than other top-notch deep learning models trained using mainstream iterative algorithms. Additionally, we've successfully used the method to solve the Colebrook equation, which describes the friction factor's complex variation with Reynolds number and roughness for fluid flow in pipes, and also the Helmholtz equation, which governs fluid oscillations in machines. This newly-developed approach provides significant practical value in a wide range of engineering applications. With its gradient-free annealing capability based on optimal metrics, the method offers a viable alternative to deep learning algorithms. Its exceptional generalization performance and the ease with which it can be applied to solve partial differential equations make it a highly useful tool. We've successfully used the method to find solutions for many differential equations and it has been successfully applied to the representation of complex functions and data. Furthermore, we've successfully used the method to play Atari games using the Procgen environment and collected its source code. This new approach to ANN weight calculation offers significant theoretical value as it represents a new class of deep learning algorithms. Its numerical solutions have also been verified to converge from different initial conditions, thereby confirming its stability and the excellent generalization performance. This new approach provides a practical solution to the ANN weight calculation problem

Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
However, the line waves' high Q factors make them suitable for supporting high Q resonances but not ideal for supporting high-speed surface modes.
This work presents the theoretical and experimental design of a line waves steerer, designed to manipulate line waves and operating in the terahertz range.
The proposed device consists of two parts: both are binary super-atom arrays that produce line waves, but with arrangements that allow for control of line waves' direction.
The study confirms the successful steering of line waves through changing their spatial structure, yielding steady state images with high intensity and good directionality.
The line waves steerer offers a new approach to controlling edge modes and expands the capabilities of active surface technologies.

In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the disordered state in Tb3RuO7 primarily to the magnetic frustrations, caused by the differing internal magnetic fields imposed by the ordered terbium atoms on the two ruthenium species, leading to distinct behaviors. Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that leverages both cause and effect features to produce labels and use them in learning a domain-independent representation. This process is reinforced by the discovery of latent confounding variables. The resulting representation enables successful tasks like regression, classification, and reinforcement learning in complex, high-dimensional settings, surpassing the performance of conventional methods. The integration of causal modelling also provides insights into the latent structures that shape the observed data. The proposed approach significantly improves the accuracy of regression and classification tasks by up to 9% and 9.5% respectively, while also offering a more detailed understanding of the data's underlying structure. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our study demonstrates the efficacy of this approach by successfully simulating the doped Hubbard model with a large number of electrons. Additionally to previous work, we showcase the ability to calculate two-particle correlation functions, achieve thermal equilibrium with an exceptionally low temperature of $0.0075t$ and access deep filling fractions. Our findings reveal exceptional agreement between simulation data and rigorous lattice quantum Monte Carlo results, thereby substantiating the sign transformation's effectiveness. Our work presents the first known implementation of a determinant correction through a deep learning approach, enabling vast scale expansions, and paves the way for tackling even more complex problems. To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains. We investigate several methods for fine-tuning, including language pairing, convergence, and mixed-precision training. Our experiments reveal that fine-tuning specific model layers can yield improved results, while models converging at a lower data density tend to perform better. Interestingly, our results show that adapting the model to unseen languages can lead to improved performance on seen languages, specifically reducing error rates by 8.5% and 4.8% for German and Korean, respectively. Moreover, the improved performance translates to a 20.5% decrease in error rate in generating sentence-order translations. Our code and model configurations are openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Universal-SpeechToolkit/BigScience-ULIT. This research was supported by the knowledge and expertise of the Universal Speech Technology consortium.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we propose Mosaic, a system that facilitates the discovery of patterns within large collections of unfalsifiable claims, such as those found on social media, by utilizing crowd sourcing. Mosaic's approach involves guiding users through a selective annotation process to identify coherent positions within the data. These annotated segments are then used to train neural language models, which can generate new text based on the learned patterns. By comparing these generated texts to existing positions, we can assess their similarity and gain insights into the underlying structure of the data. Through human-AI collaborations, we can refine our findings and explore their significance. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we will investigate the structure of comments posted on New York Times articles and the views expressed on Twitter. Our experiments have shown that, even with minimal human input, Mosaic can identify and replicate complex patterns within large datasets. Additionally, we will examine the ethical implications of seeking structure in subjective content and how our findings might contribute to applications in information retrieval, combing the web for relevant positions on various topics. Mosaic could also be applied to other challenging tasks, such as fact-checking, understanding public opinions, and summarizing large discussions. To facilitate replication, we will make our code and annotated dataset available. To investigate the learning potential of unfalsifiable text, we employed a variety of baseline models and evaluated their performance using both Mosaic-generated training data and standard approaches. Our results have shown that, even with minimal human input, Mosaic can produce a range of leading baseline models. It is worth noting that our annotation process is designed to identify coherent positions within the data and can also be applied to other text classification tasks to produce unique training datasets. To address the challenge of unfalsifiable text, we also investigated the use of Mosaic in conjunction with state-of-the-art neural language models, which can learn patterns directly from the data distribution. Our experiments have shown that Mosaic can enhance the learning potential of these models, particularly when working with large collections of text. To further demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we will also evaluate the performance of Mosaic in more realistic scenarios, using a dataset of social media posts on COVID-19. Our results have shown that Mosaic can produce high-quality training data, which can be used to improve the accuracy of neural language models in semi-supervised and domain adaptation

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework leveraging social media. It addresses spatial resolution ambiguity through a quad-tree based method that segmentates regions based on data density, and uses statistical analysis incorporating the Poisson distribution to highlight anomalies in post density. Furthermore, event duration is determined by aggregating consecutive time intervals with shared spatial areas. An added filter is incorporated to remove spam, false, or inaccurate events. The framework incorporates entity-based analysis to evaluate event credibility and reliability. Evaluation is performed using multiple datasets for distinct cities, including Melbourne, London, Paris, and New York, and is benchmarked against existing approaches employing fixed spatial divisions and clustering algorithms. Assessment of recall and precision are manually computed, and a novel metric called strength index is proposed to evaluate event accuracy. Results demonstrate that the presented framework achieves better performance compared to benchmark methods. An implementation of this framework is available as open-source software called Traipse, enabling real-time event detection and updating. It offers a web interface for visualizing and querying social media events, and can be accessed at traipse.io. Future research directions are also discussed. By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability. Our source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jihun1122/BaRNN. 

Keywords: Machine Learning, deep neural networks, Bayesian learning, adversarial training, robustness certification. 

Long Text: Most practical applications of deep neural networks prefer models that are both accurate and secure from potential attacks. Training Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) provides benefits in uncertainty measurement and robustness assessment; however, achieving both accuracy and certifiable security in BNNs remains a significant challenge. The process of training BNNs involves minimizing the evidence lower bound (ELB) results in poorly trained tail weights and reduced certification reliability. This issue is compounded by the sensitivity of ELB to data quality - minor data corruptions can significantly harm certification reliability. Furthermore, integrating data augmentation to bypass the sensitivity problem leads to increased training complexity and higher certification costs. This research introduces a new training method for Bayesian Neural Networks that both improves accuracy and certifiable security, addressing issues of tail weight imbalance and the sensitivity to data quality. The approach involves developing a robust cross-entropy loss to achieve both goals. The method was successfully tested on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jihun1122/BaRNN. 

Keywords: Machine Learning, deep neural networks, Bayesian learning, adversarial training, robustness certification.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our cumulative sum technique achieved significant improvements, demonstrating the potential of natural language processing to predict a rumor's spread. By combining these approaches, we can more accurately forecast a rumor's spread, ultimately enabling more effective online crisis governance. This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed a widely used hyperspectral dataset, paired with a robust pixel classification algorithm (SVM), to ensure reliable results. Our findings show that PCA, KPCA, and ICA methods perform similarly across different compression rates, achieving nearly complete reconstruction of original features with minimal compression. In contrast, AE and DAE achieve superior results, particularly at moderate compression rates (up to 96%), outperforming PCA, KPCA, and ICA in classification performance while surpassing PCA and KPCA in reconstruction error. Notably, AE outshines DAE in classification performance, but lags behind DAE in reconstruction error. Our study promotes the use of unsupervised dimensionality reduction techniques, particularly AE, to enhance pixel classification in remote sensing applications. Additionally, our findings suggest that PCA, KPCA, and ICA can be efficiently employed when comprehensive reconstruction of original features is crucial. Conversely, AE and DAE can be preferentially used when high classification performance and efficient pixel compression are achieved with minimal loss of feature information. Furthermore, our study's code and datasets have been made publicly available to foster replication of this research. We hope this study contributes to the evolution of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction and compression. We expect these findings to be extrapolated to applications beyond remote sensing and to facilitate the development of new techniques in this field. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language models, specifically bidirectional LSTMs, and to examine the advantages of network compression through the spatial and temporal trimming of model parameters. We demonstrate that a highly accurate NLP model can be successfully compressed into a much denser network, requiring significantly fewer parameters and temporal iterations to achieve the same results. Furthermore, our findings also reveal that Compressed LSTMs can outperform traditional LSTMs in certain NLP applications. We posit that the superiority of the compressed models over their traditional counterparts may be attributed to the improved model generalization capability resulting from the imposition of a strong regularization effect during the network parameter reduction process. ProCS is calibrated with the results of high-level quantum mechanical calculations, achieving remarkable agreement in predicting the amide proton chemical shifts of a small protein with a minimal error rate of 0.25 ppm (highly accurate predictions >90%). The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on loss functions often overlooks thorough evaluation, opting for intuition or experience-guided selection. This study seeks to establish a more systematic approach to loss function evaluation, focusing on how different loss functions affect performance in a specific problem context. To this end, we examined the performance of seven leading loss functions across six benchmark datasets. Our results reveal that no single loss function emerges as the best choice across all datasets. Rather, the optimal loss function appears to depend on the specific data, task, and hyperparameter settings. Furthermore, we found that combining multiple loss functions can be detrimental, often resulting in decreased performance and regularization effects. Our research suggests that future research should prioritize a thorough evaluation of loss functions, considering various problem contexts and hyperparameter settings. Additionally, we found that the current benchmark dataset collection lacks diversity, hindering comprehensive evaluation, and propose a future direction to address this limitation by expanding the collection with more diverse datasets. The proposed research agenda and code are available on GitHub for reproducibility.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also inherently heuristic. Within the context of a theoretical framework developed by Kraichnan, a new Hamiltonian-based analysis is applied to parquet's structure in the context of fermionic particles, resulting in a natural formation of the theory's underlying equations through its canonical representation. This approach reveals the inherent connection between the conserving properties of the derived scattering amplitude and the traditional parquet theory. Although the derived amplitude conserves properties at a microscopic level, it does not maintain symmetry. In contrast, the traditional amplitude maintains symmetry but fails to conserve properties at any level. Ultimately, the decision to use one amplitude over the other is determined by the specific requirements of the system under consideration rather than its adherence to a theoretical framework. In practice, both amplitudes are capable of effectively describing both ground and thermal states as well as dynamic processes, although they may be computed at varying levels of approximation. Currently, the traditional amplitude is used more frequently in statistical physics applications. In contrast, the Hamiltonian-based analysis is more suited to describing the behaviors of small systems and may offer a more natural approach to describing both ground and excited states. A new application of the theoretical framework is proposed to study the behaviors of electrons in a lattice structure. Although the derived amplitude is sensitive to the details of its canonical representation, it is argued that certain characteristics of its structure hold true across different representations and imply the existence of certain low-energy states in any system composed of interacting fermions. In particular, in any system composed solely of fermions, a pair-based interaction results in the formation of low-energy states that are inherently paired. Furthermore, in any system where pair-based interactions are zero-order stable, a low-energy state composed of non-interacting elements does not exist. The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms a semimetallic superfluid. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, yet the current computational methods are unable to accurately predict the properties of the resulting superfluid. In this study, a new numerical approach is developed to describe the phenomenon of exciton condensation within a semimetal. This method incorporates the finite-temperature density functional theory and employs a semimetallic superfluid model to describe the pairwise interactions between electron-hole pairs. Furthermore, the theoretical framework is applied to the study of exciton condensation in the single-layer transition-metal dichalcogenide material TiSe2. Our findings show that the recently developed superfluid model outperforms the density functional theory in accurately predicting the properties of the excitonic ground state. A deep understanding of the role of electron-hole pairing in the superfluid is also gained through our investigations of the distribution function and pairing tensor of the electron-hole pairs. Our studies suggest that the pairing of these pairs is primarily mediated by long-range kinetic energy interactions rather than van der Waals interactions. Finally, our calculations demonstrate that the excitonic ground state in TiSe2 exhibits a characteristic energy scale of approximately 0.5 eV, with a possibility of modifying this energy through the incorporation of external stresses. Our research provides a new theoretical framework for the numerical simulation of exciton condensation and offers valuable insights into the material science of transition-metal dichalcogenides. Additionally, our study sparks the idea that exciton condensation could serve as a new mechanism for the generation of novel states in these materials, potentially even rivaling ferroelectricity in its ability to trigger phase transitions. Our work concludes by suggesting that the resulting excitonic ground states could potentially be characterized through the use of spectroscopic microscopies, such as pump-probe electron microscopy and photoemission spectroscopy. Our study offers a new theoretical perspective on the electronic structure of transition-metal dichalcogenides and provides a new understanding of their electronic properties. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two alternative formulations expressed in the Computational Ludics language. This modification enables a fresh exploration of the concepts underlying the Curry-Howard correspondence, specifically the interplay between proof and computation. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Additionally, our approach's adaptability allows for integration with learning methods employing static images without requiring further modification. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear Markov decision process and finding that even with the adversary only modifying the reward in each data tuple, a certain threshold of optimality gap cannot be avoided. Conversely, in contrast to robust supervised learning, which has seen significant breakthroughs with little dimension increase, and contrast to robust offline RL with the assumption of data corruption affecting states, we found that no method can do better than the worst-case scenario when the corruption affects actions. However, we discovered that using a small amount of data that is off-limit to the adversary can help in solving this problem, and this result is validated by experiments conducted on various datasets, including both synthetic and real-world data. Additionally, we introduced an approach called AugRL that can help in solving this problem by combining off-limit knowledge with on-limit data, and this method is further tested and validated. Importantly, we found that off-limit data can be obtained through simple exploration under specific conditions without requiring any further assumptions. This important finding enables us to validate the effectiveness of AugRL in a set of real-world applications. Lastly, we presented an approach called C-AUGRL that can help in solving this problem by combining off-limit knowledge with on-limit data in conjunction with certain constraints that help in reducing the impact of adversity, and this method is further tested and validated. This comprehensive body of work contributes to the area of robust offline RL and provides new avenues for exploration. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm. Lastly, we discuss the challenges and limitations of extending these results to more complex situations, including nonlinear problems and multiple dimensions. Important tools used in this research include a dual problem with a nonlinear equation and a boundary control problem with a nonlinear boundary condition. To find the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm, we use an iterative algorithm based on the L^1-projection of the solution to a nonlinear equation onto the measurable trivial set. This research primarily relies on estimating the L^2-norm of the solution to a nonlinear equation with a boundary control, which requires proving that certain coefficients are logarithmically convex under specific conditions. To achieve this, we take the derivative of the equation for the solution to a nonlinear equation with a boundary control, applying the integration by parts trick and relying on the logarithmic convexity of certain coefficients to derive desired estimates. Additionally, we discuss the relation between the imaginary and real parts of analytic functions, which is useful for estimating the L^2-norm of the solution to a nonlinear equation. To investigate the properties of certain operators, we examine the distribution of zeros in the Riemann z-plane and the singularities of holomorphic functions, which are essential for understanding the spectrum of certain compact operators and the behavior of L^2-functions. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison. Based on our findings, we suggest revising the focus from generic out-of-distribution detection to specific types of out-of-distribution data, such as background and semantic shifts, to facilitate the development of targeted detection methods. Two new methods were proposed to improve performance on background shift detection and accommodate the increasing reliance of deep learning models on large quantities of data. The proposed methods achieve notable improvements in background shift detection, with our model outperforming the previous best model by 11.3% on Cola. The proposed models, along with the corresponding technical details and the OODChallenge dataset, can be accessed at https://github.com/huutingying/Background-OUT-of-Distribution. Eight leading teams in the area have participated in the 2nd Text Out-of-Distribution Detection Challenge, with their results and being hosted by https://challenge.aihub-bj.org/index.php/2021/02/22/text-ood-2nd-challenge. The winning paper will be published at the 8th International Conference on PAKDD. The empirical analysis provided in this paper can be utilized as a guide for researchers and developers to improve the detection of out-of-distribution examples, with specific examples including background and semantic shifts, entropy-based methods, and early stopping. Additionally, we showed that pre-training deep learning models using large amounts of data would lead to inaccurate out-of-distribution predictions, which can be rectified by incorporating an encoder for pre-trained models and utilizing early stopping. Despite their potential to drive molecular machines of the future, their theoretical modeling is understudied. Here, we create a mathematical model for simulating these systems and verify its validity by applying it to a renowned molecular motor, where the model accurately reproduces existing experimental findings. Furthermore, we utilize the model to extract hard-to-determine microscopic properties and examine the influence of electric currents. The analysis shows that while non-conservative forces might play a significant role under certain conditions, they appear to be unimportant in the specific case at hand. However, conservative forces stemming from these electric currents could substantially impact the system's dynamics. Lastly, we explore the scenarios where the system's dynamics becomes driven by its own conservative forces, and find that the averaging of tunneling events yields a stochastic process compatible with that observed experimentally. To achieve this, we derive novel expressions for the conditional averages of tunneling events. By applying these to the studied system, we successfully reproduce the observed behavior, and the resulting model is validated. Overall, our proposed model facilitates the theoretical examination of artificial molecular motors, enabling the exploration of their potential to drive autonomous molecular motors in the absence of electric currents. Additionally, we believe that this model can be adapted to analyze other molecular motors and may be useful in studying non-electrically driven Brownian machines as well. It is also possible that future artificial molecular motors will be insulators rather than conductors, and we suggest that in such cases, the system might exhibit quantum behavior due to interactions at the atomic level, and this could potentially be modeled utilizing a mathematical representation of the system's microstructure. Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how complex this transformation can be. Notably, this outcome contradicts traditional transducer equivalences, which were shown to be indeterminable in certain scenarios. The proof utilizes a previously developed technique to establish a connection between two-way and one-way transducers, revealing a refined understanding of transducer equivalences. Furthermore, we examine the limitations of this result, highlighting certain model variations where a similar equivalence check can be accomplished efficiently, while others remain undecidable. Lastly, we investigate the same problem in the context of on-line (reading the input as it comes) and off-line (receiving the entire input at once) transducers, establishing decidable and undecidable cases for both models. In particular, we find undecidability for a specific class of non-deterministic one-way off-line transducers when considering complex decision problems involving context-free languages. This undecidability stands despite the best-effort model, which was shown to be impossible to decide. In contrast, we present a decision procedure for another class of non-deterministic one-way off-line transducers, specifically showing that equivalences can be determined efficiently for these models. This outcome is facilitated by a novel simulation technique that transforms an equivalent two-way off-line transducer into an one-way off-line transducer. The latter's property of being in a specific class of minimal deterministic transducers also plays a crucial role. In particular, we demonstrate that any two-way off-line transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way off-line transducer with a complexity bound of O(n), where n represents the input size. This transformation involves an algorithmic process, which we describe as finding the least complex solution for a given right-linear grammar. The latter is shown to be equivalent to a specific model of two-way off-line transducers. In doing so, we present an alternative proof for a previously demonstrated property. In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$. Our objective is to determine the fastest algorithm for computing the cumulative sum of these vectors under a specific norm, a problem which has a known brute-force solution with a time complexity of $O(|D|^n)$. Our main contribution is to demonstrate that this computational complexity can be improved to $O(n \cdot |D|^{\lceil n/2 \rceil} \log^2 |D|)$. To achieve this, we introduce an application of Fourier sampling for vector functions and use it to develop an efficient algorithm for our convolution computation. The complexity of our algorithm can be further optimized using common number theoretic techniques. The resulting efficient algorithm can be applied to various problems in number theory and coding theory. As an example, we show that it allows for a $n$-dimensional meet-in-the-middle attack on elliptic curves with a complexity of $2^{160.5}$, significantly faster than the brute-force $2^{160}$. Additionally, we propose an alternative implementation using lattice reduction that could provide valuable insights in scenarios where the complexity of our main algorithm and that of the brute-force method are close. The concepts and techniques used in this work may have independent applications. Lastly, we suggest that the problem could also be tackled using the Fourier inversion approach, exemplifying the versatility of the problem with possible solutions. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. We also explored how various factors, including the duration of exposure and characteristics of the aerosolized pathogens, might influence the comparison of our detailed model to the simpler 'well mixed' model, with a view to informing public health policies governing urban transportation systems. Additionally, we were able to derive expressions for key variables, such as the concentration of aerosol particles and the probability of infection, in terms of the parameters of our model. These expressions were found to be applicable across a wide range of conditions and were consistent with our previous numerical results. We hope that, through highlighting the limitations of the 'well mixed' model in predicting disease transmission on urban buses, this study will contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of airborne pathogens spread and help to guide public health strategies for urban transportation systems. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program violations. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all the mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq proof assistant, which did not introduce any additional axioms into the system. From these formal proofs, we were able to derive verified and executable OCaml and Haskell code for double-sided auctions. To validate the practical value of our research, we successfully tested the verified code using real market data from an exchange to automatically identify potential program violations. Our research is the first to provide fully formalized correctness proofs for double-sided auctions handling multiple quantity trade requests. Moreover, this research is the first to derive verified and executable OCaml and Haskell code for double-sided auctions, including automatic violation checking. By applying our research to an actual exchange, we were able to discover program violations that had not been previously detected. As a result, this research may contribute to improving the safety of financial exchanges' matching algorithms. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases where strong nonlinearity affects its accuracy. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, but it is limited in its ability to capture long-term behavior due to its focus on dimensionality. We introduce a kernel-based approach to generating dynamic models that combines the strengths of both techniques, allowing for the identification of both linear and nonlinear dynamics using optimized kernels. By applying our approach to several challenging systems, including a planar wing in a wind tunnel and a simulated 3D airfoil, we have successfully obtained high-accuracy reduced-order models. Furthermore, we have converted our findings into a sparse equation form, yielding reduced-order models of less complexity than the original systems. Our study demonstrates that reduced-order models derived from LANDO models exhibit increased accuracy and longer timescales compared to models generated through sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics. This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse. Our research paves the way for further investigation into the origin and development of millisecond pulsars, while also highlighting the pivotal role that accretion-induced collapse plays in shaping the stellar evolution of binary star systems. Additionally, we incorporate the recently observed millisecond pulsar J17481-4446 with a spin period of 5.39 ms and magnetic field of 1.79 x 10^10 G, demonstrating that its origin could be attributed to an accretion-induced collapse resulting from a 2.35 Msol white dwarf. Our analysis is further expanded to evaluate the observational parameters of millisecond pulsars in the globular cluster NGC 6703, yielding a spin period of 1.84 ms, magnetic field of 1.16 x 10^10 G, and mass of 1.31 Msun for the pulsar at its cluster distance. A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future. The key to this approach lies in using a suitable Lagrangian multiplier method for nonlocal positions, along with an application of the Euler-Lagrange equations to the entire motion interval. The paper demonstrates that, in certain situations, the constructed constants of motion can provide crucial information about the solutions' behavior over extended time periods. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining both short-term and long-term memories.
The short-term memory in MemoNav stores dynamic agent trajectories, updated based on the distance to the desired goal, while the long-term memory stores static images sampled from the agent's path.
To prevent forgetting, MemoNav combines both memories using a pre-trained encoder and assigns confidence scores to guide the retrieval of informative past images.
Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of MemoNav over state-of-the-art navigation methods, with its ability to generalize to new goals and environments unseen during training. 
Additionally, MemoNav's performance outclasses other methods with its ability to learn from demonstrations containing multiple objectives. 
The code for MemoNav is publicly available on our GitHub repository, https://github.com/DeepMind/MemoNav. 
Video testimonials are available on our DeepMind STEM Education website, https://www.deepmind.com/learning.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) by reusing the same licensed spectrum. However, these cells' capabilities were insufficient to support future applications like virtual reality and augmented reality. As a result, operators have sought unlicensed spectrum in the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band, with LAA being the name later assigned by 3GPP. Recent and ongoing LAA deployments predictably rely heavily on Wi-Fi, which is why understanding the technology and its applications is essential. This article delves into the history and use of unlicensed spectrum in the 5 GHz band and provides a comprehensive overview of LAA and Wi-Fi development. Following this, we discuss mode combining and switching techniques used in hybrid LAA/Wi-Fi networks, including IC and CC. We also examine the key challenges posed by WCET in large-scale deployment: determining the optimal WCET policy; managing the FPC problem; and mitigating the adverse effects of IC and CC on performance. Furthermore, we explore the future of small cells in 6G research, highlighting areas like reconfigurable backhauling, the utilization of large handover areas, and dynamic frequency leasing. Additionally, we discuss the future of unlicensed spectrum in the 6 GHz band and the essential role small cells will play in its successful implementation. Given the far-reaching implications of reconfigurability, we conclude by highlighting its potential to radically transform the architecture of future mobile networks. In the end, we summarize the key future directions for small cell research in 6G. This article was submitted to IEEE Future Touch: 6G Research Summit.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2020 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS, aiming to verify factual information and locate supporting evidence within tabular scientific data. The comprehensive dataset comprised 981 manually crafted tables and an automatically generated collection of 1980 tables, encompassing over 180,000 statements and more than 16,000 annotated evidence references. This task comprised two primary sub-tasks. Sub-task A required participants to verify whether a statement was substantiated, contradicted, or remained inconclusive relative to a given table. Meanwhile, sub-task B involved pinpointing the specific table cells that served as evidence to support the given statement. A graph's beta_k is used to study the space of all possible sets that pinpoint locations in the graph with a bounded distance. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating different architecture designs. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. This paper proposes a parallelized simulation environment based on SystemC for RISC-V multi-core platforms that incorporate multiple computing-in-memory accelerators for neuromorphic computing. The authors also investigate and demonstrate various simulation architectures for integrating these accelerators, comparing the efficiency gains against conventional sequential simulation approaches. The experimental results show that with 64 CPU cores, the parallelized simulation platform can accelerate simulation speed while maintaining accurate results. The simulated-platform latency shows near-linear growth with the number of computing-in-memory accelerators. The findings indicate that by partitioning the simulation tasks and exploiting multi-core capabilities, the proposed system can substantially improve simulation efficiency for complex neural network applications. The research provides valuable insights for developing efficient simulation tools for evaluating various architecture designs. The proposed simulation environment and parallelized code are now available on GitHub for the benefit of the research community. The platform supports flexible integration of various accelerators and can be customized to different hardware configurations, enabling the simulation of different architectural variations. Moreover, the authors successfully demonstrated the simulation of a complex deep convolutional neural network on a platform designed for actual hardware implementation, showcasing the validity and efficiency of the proposed simulation environment. The research utilized the riscv-fpga Open Source Platform and the LightCube project for the simulation and parallelization environment. The authors also utilized TensorFlow for the neural network simulations. The research was based on the following objectives: To validate the correctness of the proposed simulation environment, the authors successfully ran various tests, including loading and executing RISC-V instructions, using the Linux kernel to delegate tasks, and simulating a parallel execution of multiple instructions. The tests demonstrated that the proposed platform maintains the original instruction sequence and does not experience any out-of-order executions. To evaluate the performance of the proposed parallelization strategy, the authors conducted multiple experiments using different numbers of computing-in-memory accelerators. The results show that the partitioning strategy achieves nearly linear speedup with minimal overhead. Furthermore, the authors observed that the latency of parallel tasks shows near-linear growth with the number of accelerators. The findings indicate that the proposed parallelization environment can substantially improve simulation efficiency while maintaining accurate results. The research provides insights into efficient architecture design by examining various integration approaches for computing-in-memory accelerators

Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from uninterpretable models, questionable reliance on imperfect
data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various
probability outcomes.
  This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the
existing Decision Trees model. These revised models are designed to learn under
conditions of uncertainty, draw conclusions in uncertain situations, produce
reliable probability distributions over potential labels, and be dissected into
clear, logical arguments that can be applied to other reasoning systems. Our
approach is heavily influenced by concepts of necessity and possibility. To test
the efficacy of Indecision Trees, we created the Necessity Logic Classification
dataset, comprising text documents annotated with necessity degrees that reflect
their true categorization. Through comparison with standard Decision Trees and
other machine learning models, we demonstrate the capacity of Indecision Trees to
preserve key features, produce highly accurate probability distributions, and
facilitate the representation of their decision-making processes via visualized
trees. Additionally, we show that Indecision Trees can be modified to learn under
different modes of uncertainty, including subjective and group uncertainties. 
Finally, we illustrate the application of Indecision Trees to several other
reasoning systems, encompassing necessity, possibility, and probabilistic logic,
as well as argumentation theory, specifically in compliance with established rules
and change of heart scenarios. Code and dataset are available for reproduction
of results at https://github.com/kkrishna/indecision-trees. Experimental findings
have been made available on https://krishnakhalsa.github.io/indecision-trees/.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by reinforcing key testing concepts through feedback. We aim to improve this aspect by introducing Testing Tutor, a platform that offers various testing pedagogies and a customizable feedback engine. An empirical study comparing the impact of traditional and conceptual feedback on two groups of sophomore students was conducted. By providing students with either code-focused or concept-based feedback using Testing Tutor, our study demonstrated that conceptual feedback led to increased code coverage, fewer redundant test cases, and improved programming grades. Additionally, our results show that testing conceptual feedback promotes deeper learning of testing design and software development principles. You can find more details on our research at https://testing-tutor.github.io/. New features to support testing-based learning in real-world projects have been added to Testing Tutor and are available for download at https://github.com/Testing-Tutor/Testing-Tutor. The project code is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/Testing-Tutor/testing-tutor-api and https://github.com/Testing-Tutor/testing-tutor-frontend. Further research is suggested to explore the effect of testing conceptual feedback on larger scales, such as in senior education and across various programming levels. Utilizing Testing Tutor, educators can now provide their students with either code-focused or testing conceptual feedback, catering to distinct learning styles and promoting testing-based education. Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study sheds light on the pivotal elements contributing to over-smoothing and offers empirical evidence validating various countermeasures to mitigate it. The research also provides a suite of created datasets and codes to facilitate further exploration. The empirical evaluation, conducted using 13 diverse graph neural networks across 7 benchmark datasets, reveals that the over-smoothing phenomenon is not solely caused by the Graph Convolutional layer but also significantly influenced by other factors such as the used graph neural network type, activation functions, and degree distribution of the graph. The study offers several countermeasures to overcome over-smoothing, including the incorporation of bypass connections, the application of residual connections, and the use of spatial self-attention mechanisms. The research also presents new insights into the relationship between the depth of Graph Convolutional Networks and their performance, as well as the distribution of degrees in graphs, which may aid in selecting suitable graph neural network configurations and degree distributions for specific tasks. The study also explores the over-smoothing phenomenon in the context of Graph Attention Networks and Simple Neural Networks. The research combines theoretical analysis with extensive empirical evaluation to deepen the understanding of the over-smoothing phenomenon and provides practical recommendations for addressing it. The research findings may also be seen as an effort to develop new graph neural networks that surpass the performance of Graph Convolutional Networks. Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, with promises of better Quality of Service. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to split profits in exchange for enhanced network performance by the ISPs. To model these negotiations, we construct a game-theoretic framework, where the ISP with the worst network performance sets a higher profit-sharing rate, while the Content Provider's decision to pay is contingent upon achieving a minimum Quality of Service level. We find that the Content Provider's willingness to pay is inversely related to the number of ISPs and the difference in their network performance. Additionally, when the Content Provider is willing to pay, its profit is inversely related to the number of ISPs and the difference in their network performance, with this willingness to pay decreasing as the difference in their network performance increases. We validate these findings through numerical analysis and compare them to existing studies, finding that our results align with those of Guimares et al. for scenarios with only two Content Providers and varying numbers of ISPs, as well as a study by Lin and Greiner when there are multiple Content Providers and a single ISP. We further demonstrate that our results can be extended to cover scenarios with more than two Content Providers through numerical analysis, finding that our findings are consistent with those of Lin and Greiner. Finally, we explore how profit-sharing is distributed among Content Providers in scenarios with multiple Content Providers and a single ISP, revealing that each Content Provider bears a fair and equal portion of the costs. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds relies on expert knowledge due to the imprecision caused by recording equipment and the variability of sound recordings themselves.  Research has been conducted to improve this process, and several methods have been developed for heart sound classification that account for various types of distortion and noise.  This paper presents a new approach, based on an existing method, that uses a specific type of deep neural network to classify heart sounds with specific characteristics.  Not only does this method address the issue of noisy recordings, but it also makes fewer assumptions about the nature of these recordings.  Performance tests were conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of this method.  Data from two sources were used for these tests, and the results show that this approach produces the highest accuracy when combined with the smallest possible linear filter.  Additionally, the method demonstrates superior performance over other, related methods when specific types of distortion are introduced to normal heart sounds.  Further work is needed to refine this approach and make it suitable for use in portable, point-of-care devices.  The code used for this research is available on a public platform for others to access and build upon.  The datasets employed for the tests are also made available for anyone to download.  The new method is termed an ANCE (Additive Noise Convolutional Encoder) network, and it has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy of heart sound classification while accounting for various types of distortion and noise. In a 2021 study, we had developed a more accurate calculation for a specific nuclear transition in $^{133}$Cs using relativistic coupled-cluster theory. Recently, Roberts and Ginges raised concerns about a part of this calculation that they disagreed with, but it aligns with earlier calculations. In response, we thoroughly justify our method and highlight that all components were treated equally, whereas other calculations relied on sum-over-states methods. Additionally, we addressed concerns about the approximate treatment of some corrections that were not the main focus, but rather included for completeness, without changing our overall conclusions, as our results hold even when replaced with a previously estimated correction value. Our findings remain consistent, confirming the original constraints for $\Delta A_{np}$ and $\Delta A_{ne}$, and providing a new limit for $\Delta A_{ee}$. We also call for more experimental research on this topic, as our calculations suggest that $^{133}$Cs could potentially constrain new physics beyond the Standard Model to a greater extent than previously thought. However, we agree with the authors that our work could be improved by directly calculating certain relativistic corrections, and welcome the opportunity to collaborate, as proposed by Roberts and Ginges, to achieve this. Please see our accompanying paper for further details on how to collaborate and improve our work. In the context of new, more precise PV measurements, our work indicates that $\Delta A_{np}$ could potentially reach $\sim 1.02\cdot10^{-10}$, largely driven by the prospects for $^{131}$Cs, as well as other atoms like $^{133}$Cs, $^{133}$Xe, and $^{132}$Cs, offering opportunities to explore CP-violation in light nuclei, as well as the properties of antineutrons. We suggest that researchers revisit our 2021 work for the details of these possibilities. We also took the opportunity to clarify our understanding of the neutrino-nucleon interaction in the context of new, non-zero $\Delta A_{ne}$. We propose that if $\Delta A_{ne}$ is discovered to be non-zero, it could be utilized to investigate whether neutrinos and antineutrinos interact differently with matter, an inquiry that has significant implications for neutrino oscillations. We acknowledge that such an understanding would necessitate a more in-depth examination of nuclear transitions, but believe that with further development, relativistic CC theory has the potential to significantly contribute to our understanding of such interactions. This mixer enhances their artistic capabilities, particularly in assembling complete compositions from disparate elements. As a testament to the Neural Painters' artistic abilities, we created a permanent online gallery showcasing their masterpieces. Our code and Neural Painters are openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/Chun-Kai/Hourly-Neural-Painters. (On GitHub, search for 'neural-painters'). This research was inspired by the 'Neural Paintings' course offered by the University of Michigan via the Coursera platform, taught by Professor David H. Ballard. We would like to extend our gratitude to him for introducing us to the world of Neural Painters. Our research complies with the principles outlined in the Robustness Guidelines suggested by the PML team. Specifically, we found the following challenges to be particularly relevant: the Limb Displacement challenge (Section 2.4) and the Semantics challenge (Section 2.5). Our research explores these challenges in more detail. We found that Neural Painters excel in Limb Displacement but struggle with Semantics. We hypothesize that GANs may employ kinematic primitives to generate brushstrokes, making them more sensitive to limb displacement. However, GANs lack semantic understanding, limiting their ability to paint objects they have not encountered during training. To address this shortcoming, we mixed Color and Semantic Mixer modules. Our experiments reveal that Neural Painters can learn to paint objects they have not seen during training, thus demonstrating their potential to learn semantic features. We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, specifically addressing CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $B$ meson decays, with the introduction of heavy flavorful vector bosons at an energy scale of $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$. If these vector bosons are substantially heavier, around $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ or above, a problem arises, as we then encounter difficulty in resolving the $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ anomaly consistently with the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ mixing constraints. However, the proposed framework is compatible with the given data within the one-sigma confidence threshold for each anomaly, with the parameter space to be examined by experiments such as NA62 and KOTO and through direct searches at the Large Hadron Collider. Furthermore, we illustrate how the proposed vector bosons can be detected directly via experiments or indirectly through loop effects, specifically potenially revealing themselves in the $B^0$ decay pattern. Lastly, we establish that, even if they participate in new physics at $1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ scales, the primary influence on the strong interaction at $100\,\mathrm{MeV}$ scales can be eliminated. Vector bosons are substantial at scales of $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ to address the anomalies, with potential discoveries to be examined through multiple methods: direct detection, via the loop effect in $\tau$ lepton decay patterns, or potentially in the $B^0$ decay pattern. Additionally, this theory is compatible with the LHC constraints; nevertheless, this theory can be validated or refuted by upcoming experiments: NA62, K, Koto, and LHCx. Moreover, we found that, to tackle the $b\to c\tau\overline{\nu}_{\tau}$ anomaly, the required coupling of the vector bosons needs to be substantial ($\sim 1$), with a significant impact on the $\tau$ lepton decay patterns, potentially within the one-sigma confidence threshold. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. We also explored the use of pre-trained models that integrate paper information, but found them to be inadequate in addressing questions that demand sensitive reasoning. As a consequence, there is now a lack of such models in the field, and the proposed QASPER dataset offers valuable resources to support the development of more effective models. It is now available online, alongside accompanying code, data, and evaluation results. We welcome contributions that can further enhance the dataset or help validate the proposed methods. Ultimately, the proposed research outcomes may hold the potential to advance research in question answering, supporting both researchers and software engineers working on related challenges. To that end, we have established a website with relevant information, including a full dataset, relevant code, and detailed results of our experiments. These resources can be accessed at: https://qasper.org/. We are now seeking input from the research community to help address questions, expand the dataset, and make it possible to answer information-seeking queries based on entire research papers, thanks in large part to the generous contributions of many talented researchers.
