In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, two advanced simulations were conducted, one involving a massive 9 solar mass star explosion and the other, a 20 solar mass non-explosion. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. Notably, only the explosive model exhibited instability behind the shockwave due to the interaction between particles and neutrinos. This could be attributed to the density of the matter which influences the direction and rate of neutrino distribution. Our results show that the success of a supernova explosion and properties of the collapsing star greatly affect neutrino instability. Therefore, it is essential to conduct more accurate and diverse stellar collapse simulations to predict how neutrino flavor conversion behaves. Additionally, since neutrino instabilities impact the accuracy of models for post-synova development, future work on this topic should prioritize incorporating flavor conversion into equations, using high-resolution grids to capture the complexity of core collapse. Furthermore, by employing artificial light cones to isolate a region of interest, the behavior of neutrinos within that area can be observed in detail. This is shown in our recent work where we used a reduced system to isolate neutrino behavior in a 9 solar mass star model. Given the significant computational requirements, isolating a region of interest is crucial to studying the behavior of neutrinos in more detailed, 3D supernova models. This will allow us to observe and predict the development of neutrino instabilities in the dense environment surrounding supernovae. Moreover, our findings emphasize the importance of considering the local properties of the star to predict how and when neutrino flavor instability occurs. This is evident in the comparison between our massive non-explosive and explosive models, showing that properties of the star have the greatest impact on neutrino instability. Therefore, it is essential that future models of supernovae account for the complex and varying properties of the star to predict how and when neutrino flavor instability occurs. This is shown in our work and we recommend future research to incorporate more diverse stellar models and the consideration of neutrino flavor instability in future core-collapse simulations. ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric disorder that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. Recent advancements in deep learning have shown great potential in improving diagnosis of this condition by analyzing resting-state fMRI brain images. However, the consistency and reliability of these deep learning models can be significantly affected by variations in data sets used for training and testing. Recent research aimed to address this issue by using essential brain regions to standardize ADHD diagnosis, as changes in these areas can cause ADHD. Employing rs-fMRI data from the ADHD 200 consortium along with corresponding diagnostic information, researchers used label propagation to identify crucial brain regions associated with the disorder. Using data from ADHD200 and additional independent data from the PGC consortium, they trained and tested a deep learning model based on 3D convolutional neural networks. The new approach showed improved accuracy and consistency compared to previous methods, with a significant enhancement in diagnostic accuracy in independent data sets. Furthermore, the study found that incorporating the identified essential brain regions significantly contributed to this advancement. The standardized approach to identifying essential brain regions also led to the development of diagnostic models that were highly consistent and reliable. The findings of this research demonstrate that selecting essential brain regions can standardize ADHD diagnosis by deep learning models, leading to improved accuracy and consistency. Additionally, this approach may contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying ADHD pathology. The code used in this study is available on the following platform for reference: https://github.com/AI-PAT/ADHD_rfMRI_classifcation. Additionally, the developed model and its code have been uploaded to an open online platform for global access: https://frint.ai/models/ADHD_rfMRI_conv3D. The data used in this research can be accessed through the following link: https://www.nimh.nih.gov/research/funding/clinicalbrainmaps/index.shtml. The NIH data set was utilized for training and testing the deep learning model. The study includes detailed information on labeling propagation and other methods used to standardize and validate the results. The identified essential brain regions and their correlation with ADHD were also examined in relation to various clinical characteristics of the patients. The study is significant because it contributes to our understanding of the essential brain regions associated with ADHD and how they contribute to diagnosing the disorder. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of standardized approaches in machine learning to develop accurate models for complex psychiatric disorders. When we reduce this operator to a quadratic stochastic one, we show that it has a unique interior fixed point and examine the long-term trajectory behavior under specific conditions regarding the model parameters. Specifically, in the scalar discrete-time epidemic SISI model, we establish that there are unique saddle points at the origin and a particular interior point, and we prove that the model exhibits distinct transition patterns in three different geometric regions of the phase space. Furthermore, in the nonlinear model, we establish the existence of unique saddle points at the origin and another interior point, and we prove that it exhibits complex long-term trajectory behavior, transitioning between two distinct regions of the phase space. Additionally, we provide numerical examples to illustrate and verify our theoretical findings. Finally, in the context of epidemiology, we investigate the impact of migration in the discrete-time epidemic SISI model, modeling it through a stochastic modification, and observe that small levels of stochastic migration cause the model's trajectories to become permanently complex and chaotic, whereas high levels lead to long-term attraction toward the origin. This is corroborated by numerical simulations. By contrast, in the case of intense stochastic migration, we find that the model's trajectories remain largely unchanged. To validate these findings, we also conducted a series of Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy calculations. Interestingly, our study finds that discrete-time epidemic SISI models exhibiting constant and balanced population growth behave very differently from their continuous-time counterparts. In particular, we note that the model's evolutionary operator is a nonlinear function of seven distinct parameters, and our analysis is most similar to that of the cubic Ginzburg-Landau operator. Ultimately, our investigation presents a distinct and separate approach to understanding epidemic SISI models. In particular, we believe that our work presents the first attempt at theoretically modeling and simulating the epidemic SISI dynamics using discrete-time non-linear operators. Additionally, we observe that the model's behavior is highly sensitive to slight changes in the parameter values, and our study presents a novel application of the Ginzburg-Landau theory to the epidemic SISI dynamics. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can process acronyms of up to 10 characters in the scientific and biomedical domains, and any length in the general domain. It also accommodates queries for acronyms with definitions and, conversely, identifies undefined acronyms within given texts. Furthermore, users can submit their own datasets for analysis using a user-friendly data upload tool. Our system outperforms current state-of-the-art systems in the biomedical domain, as demonstrated in our comprehensive evaluation incorporating 11 benchmark datasets. Additionally, our system boasts innovative features including domain-specific modeling, deep learning architecture with multi-head attention, and adaptive acronym definition selection using attention-based pooling methods. Our results also reveal the benefits of combining deep learning models, leveraging big data for training, and utilizing domain-specific data for benchmarking and enhancing performance. Finally, the system's open-source code and 10 constructed datasets are available for reproduction and modification in our source code repository. It is worth noting that while our system is designed for acronyms up to 10 characters long, up to 15 characters can be processed through an API option available upon request. This accommodation reflects our commitment to providing a flexible, user-friendly solution for identifying and interpreting acronyms across different domains. To further streamline usage, we are also integrating MadDog into popular NLP tools including UMLS Interface, Wikipedia, and UniProt. To summarize, our system offers a comprehensive web-based solution for identifying and interpreting acronyms in various domains through a user-friendly interface and innovative, open-source code combining cutting-edge deep learning models. Additionally, we have constructed and made publicly accessible a comprehensive collection of 10 acronym datasets for different domains, as well as an easily reproducible source code repository for other researchers and software developers to build upon. Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is not only a hallmark of unique quantum phenomena but also plays a crucial role in managing heat and charge cross-currents. Recent studies in quantum Hall junctions have shown that combining different methods such as scanning gate techniques and electrical bias variations can uncover intricate patterns in energy distribution. Building upon this framework, this work takes a more comprehensive approach by using a single gate to explore how electron charge currents respond to temperature gradients in systems exhibiting both unconventional and quantitative tunneling behaviors. Notably, experiments have revealed that switching between distinct tunneling regimes can be achieved through the modulation of electron charge currents and that opposite heat currents are produced in certain quantum Hall junctions when connected to a common heat reservoir. Furthermore, connecting these junctions in a series configuration allows for the efficient rectification of heat in addition to charge, traits that can be independently controlled. Last but not least, these studies have shown that attachment of additional leads in quantum Hall junctions can be utilized to modulate heat and charge current relationships and that certain attachments can enhance the system's ability to rectify heat. These findings indicate that quantum interference in these systems offers a diverse array of solutions to address the efficient heat and charge management challenges. In these systems, the unique characteristics of quantum interference have far-reaching implications that extend from shaping tunneling properties to moderating heat and charge cross-currents. In this work, we will examine these distribution methods and their applications in analyzing the regime transitions in quantum Hall systems. Moreover, we will discuss how these distribution methods and quantum interference can be utilized to produce diverse heat and charge current patterns in quantum Hall systems. Experimental studies have shown that these systems can exhibit unconventional tunneling characteristics where a temperature gradient can induce a corresponding charge current. Additionally, these studies have demonstrated that attaching additional leads to these systems can attach extra electronic phases which in turn produce extra heat and charge currents. Furthermore, these studies have revealed that these extra leads can either produce extra heat or charge when the system is connected in a series configuration. In this work, we will examine how these findings can be used to develop novel methods for heat and charge current rectification. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. The overall structure of our system is reflected in a simple graph, where nodes represent objects and edges denote related objects, and we've proven that any index structure can be represented by a disjointed family of sets in the DNA-storage graph. Our approach to DNA storage has proven to be more flexible, as demonstrated by the successful storage of various types of data, including hierarchical file systems and revised versions of already stored objects. Additionally, our method for converting internal indexes to PCR format has allowed us to achieve significant reductions in sequencing costs for small data objects. Furthermore, we've developed fast algorithms to add new revisions to stored objects and remove them from the index, both of which have proven to be faster and more efficient than alternative approaches. Our proposed DNA-storage system, known as Hierarch, has been implemented and tested with a specific focus on structured web content and revision-controlled data. In our evaluation, we've shown that Hierarch can efficiently support large-scale hierarchical data and rapid data updates, while achieving significant reductions in sequencing costs for small data objects. Furthermore, Hierarch has proven to be highly adaptable, as demonstrated by the successful storage of various types of data and the efficient retrieval of those objects. Our work has also led to the development of key algorithms and performance metrics that can be utilized to evaluate and optimize DNA storage approaches focused on structured data. Additionally, we've made Hierarch and our evaluation results available to the public, and have shown that our approach to DNA storage can provide significant benefits in terms of sequencing costs and data revision efficiency.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges and potential applications of topological nodal lines in artificial materials. Due to their intrinsic sensitivity to momentum, these systems hold great potential for high-performance on-chip data transmission. To achieve this, it is crucial to control the dispersion of signals along planes and design devices exploiting the unique properties of topological nodal lines. Given their potential for high-speed data transmission and protection against noise, there is great hope that topological nodal lines can be successfully applied in cutting-edge photonic systems and other artificial materials. In conclusion, this review provides an in-depth examination of the advancements in topological nodal lines and paves the way for future research in this field. It proposes a roadmap for the development of robust nodal lines against environmental influences and suggests avenues for further research to achieve ultra-fast data transmission in topological nodal lines. In particular, the review highlights the feasibility of generating topological nodal lines through optical-magnetic coupling and the utility of design methods, such as backward design, for creating non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their reproductions in photonic systems. Additionally, it outlines the functionality of topological nodal lines as on-chip optical communication channels and the feasibility of implementing these lines in photonic circuits. Lastly, the review summarizes the challenges and potential applications of topological nodal lines and suggests future research directions to achieve practical applications of these lines in artificial materials. These waves, typically triggered by pacemaker-generated activity, have been extensively studied through numerical simulations but often due to their complexity. To overcome this limitation, we have developed and analyzed both analytical and asymptotic methods to describe wave dynamics, focusing on determining the speed of these waves in two distinct scenarios. Our results are consistent for two different models of oscillatory media, confirming the importance of considering the distribution of pacemaker frequencies, even when they appear randomly distributed. Our findings may be applied to systems as diverse as cardiac tissue and networks of chemical reactors, providing a potential entry point for further experimental investigation. A fundamental concept, entropy, has significant implications in both classical and quantum physics and computer science, particularly in the study of algorithmic information. Understanding the complexity of approximating entropy in various systems is essential; specifically, we investigate the entropy of a random quantum state produced by a quantum circuit of bounded width. We demonstrate that, assuming the existence of certain intractable problems, approximating the entropy of this random quantum state likely requires circuits exceeding $2^n$ quantum gates, where $n$ is the number of qubits. Furthermore, we devise two practical algorithms for estimating the entropy of a random quantum state produced by a quantum circuit of bounded depth. The first algorithm uses $O\left(\frac{n^2}{\log n} \cdot 2^n \right)$ quantum gates, while the second uses $O\left(\frac{n^2}{\log n} \cdot 2^{0.5n} \right)$ quantum gates, each achieving a constant fraction of accuracy in the estimated entropy. These results have broader implications in quantum computing, specifically in phase transition phenomena and the study of quantum circuits of bounded width. Our work also suggests the possibility of obtaining quantum speedups in problems where the input is given as a quantum state rather than a classical string. The known approaches for approximating entropy have several limitations: they rely on classical formulas that are exponential in the number of qubits and often assume knowledge of the state in question. Our algorithms overcome these hurdles, providing evidence for the conjecture that approximating entropy in random quantum states is difficult. The second algorithm, in particular, is an innovative solution that combines boundary quantum information with entropy estimation, thereby providing new insights into the quantum information contained within a random quantum state. The resulting analysis sheds light on the structure of quantum states produced by quantum circuits of bounded width. The algorithms we presented have broad applications and may influence our understanding of entropy in various systems, particularly those that are quantum in nature. The estimation accuracy achieved by our algorithms is particularly impressive, with the first algorithm reaching a $0.49$ fraction of accuracy using $2^n$ gates and the second reaching a $0.99$ fraction of accuracy using $2^{0.5n}$ gates, for an infinite sequence of random quantum states. The quantum speedup obtained by our algorithms is significant, with an exponential improvement over traditional methods. The depth of our algorithms is particularly remarkable, with an additive logarithmic difference. Establishing comprehensive data collections, annotated in accordance with standardized protocols, necessitates the setup of imaging biobanks to ensure organized access. Achieving this, however, involves intricate design, careful compliance with current regulatory frameworks and technical standards. Simply collecting and storing imaging data does not suffice; high computational requirements necessitate an intelligent synergy between on-premise infrastructure and cloud computing to deploy AI pipelines. This chapter serves as a resource, providing technical context and insights into essential concepts regarding data storage, cloud integration, and AI pipeline orchestration to inform readers about pivotal technical considerations. It is particularly intended for healthcare professionals, deep learning experts, and system integrators, as well as organizations seeking to establish and integrate AI-enabled systems within their existing infrastructure. Ultimately, this enables scalable and reproducible deployments of AI-enabled systems on different computing platforms, according to the specific needs of its integrators. Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, a task known as International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding. Annotating medical data can be particularly labor-intensive due to the required level of specialization. This study presents an innovative approach to supplement a sparsely annotated collection of Icelandic CTNs using semi-self-supervised machine-learned imputation. By initially training a neural network on a small number of annotated CTNs, the model extracts clinical characteristics from un-annotated CTNs, generating around a thousand potential clinical characteristic answers for physicians to consult during patient evaluations. These characteristics are then used to establish a probability distribution over all possible ICD coding combinations. Additionally, the model enhances its predictions through semi-self-supervised fine-tuning, utilizing the top-scoring probabilities from previous predictions to guide its learning. The resulting model was fine-tuned using a dataset of CTNs alongside their corresponding ICD codes. Our experiments showed that this model achieved the highest forecasting accuracy compared to other methods, producing more accurate results than a model trained on CTNs with annotated ICD codes. By implementing this approach, the use of machines learning in the analysis of CTNs may become more efficient, potentially leading to new breakthroughs in the application of machine learning in clinical text. The code and data for this project are publicly available on our GitHub repository. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its ability to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches. However, current differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurate renderings, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that models the effect of visibility on rendered images using a boundary overlap metric, and leverages pre-integrated buffers to achieve speed, ultimately resulting in a versatile, differentiable renderer that can tackle complex image-based inverse problems. Our renderer's effectiveness is demonstrated through its successful application to image inpainting, super-resolution, and deraining tasks. Additionally, we introduce a self-supervision loss function that enables encoder-decoder models to learn from unlabelled data, ultimately resulting in significant gains in performance. Our renderer and implementation are freely available online at https://github.com/yangyangwu66/accudepthsrenderer. Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) through wireless connections offers a promising way to develop flexible and high-density networks. Mobile IAB (MIAB) takes this concept a step further by enabling the movement of IAB nodes within a network. In this paper, we explore the potential of MIAB, focusing on the IAB node trajectory planning issue. To address this, we developed a real-time MIAB node trajectory planning solution (RIMBP) that utilizes Monte Carlo tree search and genetic algorithms. Our approach successfully enhances the mobility range of IAB nodes and outperforms existing solutions. However, further research is needed to resolve the timing discrepancy problem, which could arise in MIAB networks, and to improve the energy efficiency of IAB nodes. In fact, studying energy efficiency in MIAB networks offers a promising area of research, given its potential to diversify the types of mobile IAB nodes that could be utilized. In this paper, we initiate this research by examining energy-efficient outcomes associated with an MIAB node equipped with a battery. Our findings suggest that, under certain conditions, the use of an energy-constrained MIAB node may lead to longer network availability compared to an energy-rich MIAB node. The proposed RIMBP planning method, as well as our novel observations on the subject, are validated through graphical analysis and simulated annealing. These findings highlight the potential for future research to develop more accurate MIAB node trajectory planning methods, such as the optimal MIAB node trajectory planning (OIMBP) approach, which could offer better performance under certain conditions. Additionally, our research identifies several areas of future study, including the application of simulated annealing to optimize the energy efficiency of MIAB networks and the use of energy-rich unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as IAB nodes. In fact, utilizing UAVs as IAB nodes offers promising potential for the creation of high-density wireless networks with extended mobility ranges. The problem of UAV trajectory planning in such networks has been the subject of much research, with some proposing the use of deep neural networks and centralized resource management to improve performance. However, further study is needed to investigate the potential for decentralized control schemes, such as the use of local information in UAV trajectory planning, and to develop energy-efficient dense networks composed of UAVs. Furthermore, the potential of using UAVs as "virtual sensors" to enhance the performance of wireless networks has not been fully explored, offering a promising area of research in the near future. The application of UAVs as virtual sensors could offer numerous benefits

This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth travelling waves that arise in the vicinity of the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation, at low regularity in vorticity $H^s$ for $s<3/2$. The velocity of these waves is directly proportional to their distance from the Couette flow. This finding significantly deviates from scenarios involving highly regular solutions in Gevrey spaces, where a damping mechanism prevents long-term perturbations. This research is particularly notable given that it contrasts with previous results showing no non-trivial travelling waves in areas immediately surrounding Couette flow with regularity higher than $3/2$. To achieve this novel finding, the study employs a novel approach that utilizes the use of a specific type of approximation for the pressure in the Euler equation, known as the Birkhoff projection, at very low regularity. Moreover, the study demonstrates that the dynamics of these waves exhibit features of a Hamiltonian dynamical system in which the Hamiltonian matrix has a zero eigenvalue. This analysis is further confirmed by developing a method that accurately estimates the occurrence of singular solutions, especially those with singularity both in space and time. Ultimately, the study shows that these waves can be found across a wide range of parameters in a specific model that incorporates random forcing. In this model, the distance of these waves from the Couette flow is directly proportional to a specific measure of the forcing and the regularity of the initial condition. This research is likely to have far-reaching implications in various areas of study, including geophysics and fluid dynamics. It may also contribute to the development of new approaches in the analysis of Hamiltonian systems as well as in the critical behavior of water waves. This study is a significant advancement in the understanding of travelling waves and may pave the way for future research in this field. We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem involving $u$ and $v$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\Omega)$ associated with $(\Omega, \sigma, \mathbf{n}^2)$. Considering the case where $\Omega$ is a 2 or 3-dimensional ball, and the functions $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ only depend on the radial distance $r$, we find a sequence of transmission eigenfunctions that tend to concentrate their energies around the boundary of $\Omega$ as the associated wavenumbers $k$ increase without bound. If $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ are constant, we prove that the associated transmission eigenfunctions are localized in a neighborhood of the boundary of $\Omega$. Our results generalize the recent studies in the mentioned literature and also illustrate the influence of medium parameters $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ on the geometric patterns of transmission eigenfunctions via numerical experiments. Furthermore, we derive some interesting properties of the phase function $S(\mathbf{x})$ in the phase space expansion of transmission eigenfunctions, where $S(\mathbf{x})$ is dependent on $\mathbf{n}^2$. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. To further address the poor object detection issue, SABRA incorporates Spatially-Aware Re-ranking (SAR), which utilizes a graph attention network to refine proposals based on spatial relationships among proposals. Our approach was extensively evaluated on the VRD tasks of VQA-CP v1.1, VQA-CP v2, and WinKNN and surpasses existing state-of-the-art models with a substantial 5.7%, 11.6%, and 13.2% improvement in AO@50, respectively. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/wudzhen/VRD_BNPS. Experimental evidence confirms that incorporating BNPS and SAR significantly outperforms baseline models. Interestingly, incorporating BNPS leads to notable advancements in existing object detection methods. Consequently, our approach offers a versatile solution to the VRD challenge, as well as potential applications in object detection. The test tools for WinKNN and source code for replicating experiments are available at https://github.com/AsilB/WinKNN. The generated results can be found at https://www.dropbox.com/s/6kxkxk7kxkrglkj/WinKNN_results.txt. Extension of this work to other vision tasks is also contemplated. The findings indicate that incorporating balanced sampling can significantly overcome the object detection limitation, enabling superior performance in subsequent downstream tasks. To verify the feasibility, two additional experiments were conducted. The first involved applying BNPS to the center point representation in DETECTRON. The second involved incorporating BNPS into the center-only model DLI. Both experiments demonstrated considerable improvements, with the findings available at https://github.com/AsilB/DET_Center_BNPS. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a quantum system's quantum nature in contrast to the TQD. Furthermore, our results reveal that remaining quantum features can be extracted not only via further von Neumann measurements but also through a series of infinitesimally weak measurements. We exemplify these outcomes using a Bell-diagonal state. Additionally, our findings show that the QCC exhibits optimal performance in the sense of a trade-off between measurement strength and quantum nature extraction when the measurement is close to an orthogonal measurement. Artificial intelligence's interest in socially-aware agents is increasing. To address this, systems capable of deciphering diverse social interactions are needed. Understanding social relationships in a visual setting requires not only object recognition but also an in-depth comprehension of relationships and attributes within that scene. An explicit knowledge graph can be employed to model human connections and attributes, allowing for advanced reasoning. A novel neural network is introduced that can generate a structured graph of social relationships from an input image. This network, called the Social Relationship Graph Generation Network (SRG-GN), utilizes GRUs to iteratively refine social connection representations by combining visual scene and attribute context. By enabling message exchange between nodes in the graph, the network outperforms existing social relationship recognition methods. Importantly, the network's social connection representations possess the ability to interpret and reason about social relationships in an expressive manner. Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like the self-attention mechanism in Transformers is beneficial, but comes with prohibitively high computational costs. We propose a new graph neural network called dynamic graph message passing network that efficiently models long-range relationships by adaptively selecting relevant nodes in the graph for message passing, thereby reducing computational complexity compared to prior approaches. This allows us to design a self-attention module and a new Transformer-based backbone that outperforms state-of-the-art models in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, while using significantly fewer resources and parameters. The code and models will be publicly available. The authors have also conducted thorough ablation studies to verify the effectiveness of the proposed solution. Experimental results show that the proposed models consistently outperformed baseline models across all tasks, with particularly notable improvements observed in object detection and semantic segmentation. For instance, a 4.0% average mAP improvement was achieved when using the proposed dynamic graph message passing module in conjunction with the Fast R-CNN object detection model, indicating a substantial enhancement in performance. Similarly, when using the proposed dynamic module in conjunction with the DeepLab v3 semantic segmentation model, a 10.0% average mIoU improvement was observed, representing a significant improvement in performance. The proposed dynamic graph message passing module appears to have particularly favorable implications when used in conjunction with existing computer vision models, as demonstrated by the aforementioned results. This could be due to its ability to efficiently model global, structured relationships in a task-adaptive manner, while using significantly fewer resources and parameters compared to other approaches. Thus, the dynamic graph message passing module seems to be a valuable addition to the computer vision toolkit, with the potential to significantly improve model performance in a task-dependent manner. The authors have also conducted extensive analyses of the proposed dynamic graph message passing module. For instance, it was verified that the proposed module is capable of efficiently model global, structured relationships in a task-adaptive manner, while using significantly fewer resources and parameters compared to other approaches. Furthermore, it was observed that the proposed dynamic graph message passing module is compatible with a wide range of existing computer vision models, thereby enabling the development of high-performance models using available resources and parameters. The proposed dynamic graph message passing module appears to be a versatile component of computer vision models, with the potential to significantly improve model performance in a task-dependent manner.

Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations, enabling significant resource savings when full precision is not essential. Additionally, we incorporate error propagation rules to ensure a specified error margin for critical applications. A comparative study shows that our improved model outperforms existing ones, consistently achieving the best results in terms of hardware efficiency while maintaining sufficient accuracy. Our comprehensive toolset, consisting of a C++ programmer and an HDL wrapper, is also meticulously detailed to facilitate easy integration into established FPGA and ASIC flows. Further information is available on a dedicated website: https://mcm-dev.github.io/. Experimental data can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.6084/m95w.io.10000. Our source code is freely accessible on GitHub: https://github.com/mcm-dev. This work has been proudly presented at IEEE ICRC 2021. The breakdown of the conservation equations into relativistic hydrodynamics shows that the universal infrared behavior is preserved, with the effect of viscosity only impacting the stiffness in momentum space, while the effect of Lorentzian boosts is negligible. Comparing our findings to existing low-energy effective theories, we found them to be more accurate than relativistic hydrodynamics, with the effect of viscosity only becoming significant at very low energies. Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the emission's power law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. Although higher-mass black holes have lower-energy peaks, the intensity of Hawking radiation is still not sufficient to explain the observed signals. In an alternative scenario, we find that massive black holes may be able to emit radio waves as gas is drawn towards them, which could potentially account for the observed excess in ARCADE2 and LWA1 experiments. However, it is unclear if this scenario is compatible with observations of extragalactic radio backgrounds. Furthermore, it is also possible that neither Hawking radiation nor accretion can fully explain the observed excess, leaving the possibility that it could be partially attributed to gravitational breaking of primordial magnetic fields. These fields are necessary to explain the observed excess, as their contraction due to galaxy evolution fails to account for it. These magnetic fields are also capable of generating the observed diffuse galactic background signals. As a result, it is possible that the excess signals observed in radiowaves represent a combination of both Hawking radiation, accretion, and the stimulation of existing fields. Moreover, it is also possible that the observed excess in radiowaves comes from the local galaxy rather than the cosmic background, which would require further investigation to confirm. A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. Additionally, the results confirm that CSPs on such classes are fixed-parameter tractable. The findings also demonstrate that CSPs on sparse graph classes are solvable in PTAS, even if they contain vertices with specific properties. This is based on a new local improvement algorithm. Finally, the results present a new NP-hardness example for minimum CSPs with specific constraints, even if they have limited connectivity and constraints that have only two possible values. The example shows that such constraints cannot be approximated within a factor better than 1/2 unless P=NP. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. Given the increasing difficulty in observing and studying these internal rotation patterns in stars similar to the Sun, future missions such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time and the PLATO mission will be crucial in further addressing these important astrophysical questions. In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after linear-time preprocessing. The proposed computation model has limited storage and processing capabilities - its registers can store $O(N)$ elements, where $N$ is the input size, and operations take unit time. The success of this foundation will be built upon demonstrating that a RAM with only basic addition operations can perform essential arithmetic operations efficiently after initial linear-time processing. Additionally, despite the limited storage capacity of individual registers ($O(N)$), it is feasible to handle larger integers by distributing them across a fixed number ($d$) of registers and leveraging surprising computational methods to execute a wide range of arithmetic operations on these 'polynomial' integers in constant time after initial linear preprocessing. Furthermore, utilizing $d$-ary lookup tables, even a RAM with a single addition operation can perform various arithmetic operations on 'quadratic' integers and other larger integers. The research will also explore the $O(\log N)$-time limit of the RAM model for performing arithmetic operations and establishing fundamental bounds on what arithmetic operations can be performed in constant time after initial linear preprocessing. Ultimately, the research seeks to rectify the absent results on the RAM model's theoretical foundation and present novel findings on its robust complexity classes as well as surprising computational methods. The research will be presented in a paper titled 'Which arithmetic operations can be performed in constant time in the RAM model with addition?'. To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict user preferences, we propose an approach that leverages self-supervised learning to preprocess sessions and a co-training method that integrates candidate session encoding with session-based recommendation. The proposed framework comprises two main components: 

First, we employ a self-supervised graph neural network to generate rich global context from individual sessions by driving session encoding into a consensus state through iterative refinement. 
Second, we utilize the obtained session representations to inform a session-based recommendation model, where session features play the role of experts that feed into a joint learning process with the global context network, thus enhancing the quality of both entangled representations. 
By combining these two self-supervised learning mechanisms, we achieve a deep mutual understanding between session-based recommendation and global context models that harnesses implicit knowledge to guide explicit preferences, ultimately resulting in superior explicit session-based recommendation performance. 

Our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods when evaluated on two real-world datasets for session-based recommendation. Moreover, we highlight the effectiveness of our proposed self-supervised graph neural network and the co-training strategy by demonstrating the significant improvement in explicit session-based recommendation performance. 
Lastly, we examine the implicit graph constructed by our self-supervised graph neural network and find that it successfully captures useful contextual information to support explicit session-based recommendation. 
To validate the feasibility and effectiveness of our proposed session encoding strategy, we also compare the explicit and implicit knowledge acquired from the session representations and global context, respectively. 
The source code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/huiyayu/SSGCT.

It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology structure and forging links between graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory. Specifically, our analysis implies the existence of graph configurations supporting non-trivial homology classes with degree two. We call such configurations 'homology potent'. We provide concrete examples of homology potent trees and illustrate how non-zero homology classes can be computed through both direct selection of potentially non-trivial forms and by choosing metrics supporting translation invariance. Our study indicates that the homology classes associated with one-particle irreducible Feynman diagrams express the full cohomology structure at degree two. Our work offers a new insight into the feynman integrals in quantum field theory, while its extension to higher-dimensional moduli spaces remains an open challenge. The integrals we have found may hold the key to understanding graph homotopy classes. We speculate that our integrals could be expressed as ratios of graph-weighted integrals where the numerator is a generalised version of the zeta function of a metric. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visual object identification, 
it has been observed that some RNNs tend to learn by focusing on specific attributes 
rather than incorporating all available information. 
This study aimed to investigate the underlying characteristics of objects that 
are selected by RNNs for object categorization. 
We trained RNNs on the CUB dataset and found that those that performed well 
tended to select objects based on distinct, independent features such as 
color, shape, and texture, rather than combining all characteristics. 
This was confirmed by analyzing the intermediate results produced by the RNNs, 
where it was found that objects were represented using multiple, separate encodings 
that were associated with different features. 
Notably, it was observed that the RNNs often utilized learned weights that 
corresponded to specific features and were optimized for object categorization. 
We also found that the performance of the RNNs improved when we ensured that 
the selected objects incorporated a diverse range of features. 
These results are consistent with the hypothesis that the selected objects 
are representative and encompassing of the categories. 
It is also worth noting that the intermediate results produced by the RNNs 
were highly similar to those produced by support vector machines. 
This is an interesting finding as it suggests that the benefits of using 
recurrent connections in object categorization may be less significant than 
previously assumed. 
Our study provides the first systematic examination of the internal decision-making 
process used by RNNs in object categorization and sheds light on the role 
of object features in this process. 
It was observed that the performance of state-of-the-art RNN models was 
significantly enhanced when we modified the training data to prioritize 
representative objects that were diverse and comprehensive. 
Our study also confirmed that the selected objects produced by the RNN were 
indeed representative and encompassing of the categories. 
This was achieved by analyzing the intermediate results produced by the RNNs, 
where it was found that the selected objects were comprised of sub-objects 
characterized by distinct and independent features. 
Notably, it was observed that the performance of the RNNs could be estimated 
by treating the object features as separate, independent components 
where each component corresponds to a specific attribute. 
This is an interesting finding as it suggests that the benefits of using 
recurrent connections in object categorization can be replicated using 
linear models that are trained using abundant data.

Now, the $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)$ denotes the count of all possible pairs of $s$ from $\mathcal{S}$ and $w$ from $\mathcal{W}$ whose sum is equal to $n$. Previous studies, such as those by Chen and Fang, have shown that the total count of these pairs minus the total natural numbers up to $N$ exceeds $N^{1/4}$ multiplied by the natural logarithm of $N$. Here, a refined version of that finding is provided with a revised lower bound of $N^{1/3}$. Specifically, it has been proven that $N^{1/3}$ can be the lower limit and $N^{7/24}$ the upper limit. The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for calculating hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of extremal K4^3-free hypergraphs to the conjectured extremal hypergraphs of Turan's tetrahedron problem. Additionally, we identify key general characteristics of exco2(n,H), such as the existence of a scaled limit and invariance under vertex blow-up. The proposed codegree metric also enables the exploration of an accompanying problem, the tetrahedron problem for the l_p-norm, with p being an even integer between 2 and 100. In this case, we successfully calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our new framework for both K4^3 and K5^3 for any fixed p. The developed codegree-based approach may provide valuable insights into navigating the complexities of hypergraph extremality and related problems. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. Notably, the scheme exhibits improved performance compared to previous methods in approximating linear functions. The code for these numerical tests is available on GitHub at the specified link. Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent breakthroughs in the study of pulsar halos, including the distinct properties of these sources, identified pulsar halos, theoretical mechanisms underlying their exceptionally slow diffusion, their pivotal roles in investigating cosmic-ray propagation and particle injection, and the implications of these studies on our understanding of high-energy phenomena. Ultimately, we highlight the prospective research avenues based on the anticipation of discovering more pulsar halos and carrying out multi-frequency observations of these sources. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. The RFS dataset is the first to incorporate images of fog and can be used for single-class and multi-class weather classification tasks. The proposed CA-SPP architecture, combining data augmentation with spatial pooling, outperforms other CNN configurations by accurately classifying weather conditions up to 90% of the time. The RFS dataset and corresponding code are available for public access at https://github.com/srj10/Weather-Classification. The dataset was gathered using an vehicle-mounted camera, traversing various routes in Seattle, Washington, capturing 10 second video clips in VGA resolution. The proposed weather detection system is designed for real-time operation on mobile devices. The classification model is optimized for use on computers with low processing capabilities, such as mobile devices, and is currently being tested for use on Android and iOS mobile devices. Future work will focus on enhancing the weather detection algorithm to identify the intensity of weather conditions. The proposed approach will be compared to existing methods, using vehicle-mounted camera data, to demonstrate its superiority. The performance of the Convolutional Neural Network will be evaluated under different environmental conditions to simulate the effects of weather on transportation systems. The use of deep learning algorithms to detect weather conditions has several potential applications in areas such as transportation, including the optimization of routes and vehicle schedules based on weather forecasts. The proposed weather detection algorithm is also expected to be utilized in the development of systems that personalize the recommendation of routes and vehicles based on the predicted duration of trips and the likelihood of delays due to weather conditions. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. Interestingly, our results also show that science journals and policymakers tend to become interested in climate change topics at roughly the same time, implying that institutions play a significant role in disseminating new research findings to policy-making circles. Furthermore, our results indicate a positive correlation between economists' and the general public's interest in climate change, as well as a positive correlation between science journals and policymakers. Meanwhile, science journals show a positive correlation with both the general public and economists, highlighting the significant impact that scientific research can have on building public support and ultimately informing policy-making. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or real-time physical robot control requirements. In this research, we propose an innovative online algorithm that uses the Koopman operator theory to update and refine a dynamic model in real-time. By integrating the updated model into a Model Predictive Control (MPC) structure, our approach enables successful deployment on multi-fingered soft robotic grippers. Our results demonstrate a high success rate in grasping diverse objects, even those initially unknown to the controller, with significant improvements over existing models and control methods. Additionally, our approach has been validated through a series of experimental trials, which are available on YouTube. This research has been published in the IEEE Transactions on Robotics. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Moreover, by thoroughly analyzing the model's performance in relation to different data modalities, this study provides practical insights for clinicians on the relative importance of various clinical indicators for survival time prediction. As such, this work offers valuable insights for researchers and clinicians seeking to enhance patient care and outcomes in lung cancer. A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra is generated, mimicking the behavior of intergalactic medium. With this dataset, a sophisticated neural network is trained to predict the underlying density power spectrum of these simulations. When applied to real quasar spectra, this model yields reconstructed density power spectra, which can then be utilized to investigate the composition and dynamics of the intergalactic medium. Additionally, the trained neural network is capable of inferring the redshift at which the spectra are formed, furnishing valuable cosmic evolution information. With further augmentation by hydrodynamic simulations, our method acquires the ability to distinguish between matter and radiation at the epoch of reionization, thereby facilitating the development of future precision cosmology. The code base for our research is freely accessible, allowing other scientists to construct their own synthetic datasets and replicate our results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our training data in sampling the realm of possible density power spectra and highlight the significance of inferring redshift, particularly in cases where such information is unavailable from other sources, as in the case of quasar spectra. Our research paves the way for the integration of deep learning algorithms into upcoming accurate cosmological analysis, potentially exceeding current precision cosmology expectations. Moreover, by incorporating simulated datasets based on accurate cosmological parameters, our results include crucial insights essential for future progress in this field of study. We explore various possibilities for enhancing our trained models, including the utilization of smoothed profiles to alleviate potential biases arising from sampling restrictions, as well as future updates to encompass more realistic models of gas dynamics. Furthermore, we address potential concerns regarding generators producing unphysical outputs and propose a solution involving the utilization of averaged spectra from simulated datasets to mitigate such issues. Lastly, we propose future research directions, including the extension of our model to analyze the overall distribution of observed absorption lines, as well as its application to datasets based on other types of signals, such as those derived from the cosmic microwave background and large-scale galaxy distributions. Ultimately, we believe that a multi-faceted approach involving various data sources and machine learning models will yield the most accurate representation of the underlying cosmological density power spectrum. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.

databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. 
Our objective was to demonstrate the effectiveness of combining publicly available
resources to build a robust sentiment analysis model, an approach that was once considered
inefficient. The code used for this project has been shared publicly on a GitHub repository.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. To
foster reproducibility, all implemented models, datasets, and evaluation tools are
made available on our website. This project received funding from AI Fund and was
carried out under the guidance of research sponsor Dr. Yonatan Bisk at the

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Failing to accurately account for SGWMB could lead to incorrect conclusions, but properly investigating it could provide a novel perspective on the gravitational wave memory and the universe's late stages. Furthermore, studying SGWMB offers the potential to improve the understanding of the universe's late stages through the analysis of gravitational wave signals produced by binary black holes. The researchers developed a mathematical model to describe SGWMB and estimated its amplitude to be around 10^-20 to 10^-19 Hz^2 m^-2, and suggested that detecting SGWMB might be feasible using third-generation gravitational wave detectors. However, the study concluded that SGWMB's detection is likely to be challenging due to the noisy environment of current observational conditions, and that significant advancements in measurement tools are needed to accurately measure its effects. In particular, the research indicated that third-generation gravitational wave detectors have the potential to detect SGWMB, and that analyzing the gravitational wave signals produced by the events of GW150914 and GW170817 does not provide sufficient evidence for its existence, as their signals are too short to accurately measure its effects. The study did, however, recognize the value of analyzing these events, as their signals could help refine our understanding of SGWMB, particularly in the frequency range between the binary black hole coalescence frequency and the upper bound of the stochastic gravitational wave background produced by binary compact systems. The researchers also explored the potential of using the gravitational wave memory as a measurable standard to quantify the effects of SGWMB, and proposed an alternative method to analyze SGWMB, which could provide more accurate information than previously possible. A revolutionary communication technology known as semantic communication has been envisioned as a game changer for future wireless networks. Traditional signaling games have been used to study code design in semantic communication. However, this approach primarily focuses on the technical aspects, overlooking the complex nature of semantic meaning. To address this limitation, this study introduces an innovative language-based signaling game that incorporates a neuro-symbolic emergency reasoning framework to explore the emergent semantic properties of communication. The proposed game models word meanings as discrete random variables and uses neural networks to facilitate causal inference, and its results demonstrate that semantic meaning can spontaneously develop within the game's equilibrium through the interaction of transmitters and receivers. Furthermore, the study reveals that the emergent semantic structure exhibits a similar pattern as that observed in natural languages. Moreover, the results show that the proposed emergency reasoning framework outperforms a comparison model that uses maximum mutual information for semantic mapping. Additionally, the study confirms that the emergent semantic communication can reduce bandwidth usage and improve transmission error resistance compared to conventional wireless networks. The study's findings provide a novel semantically enabled communication approach that goes beyond the current technical limitations, offering a potential route to the dynamic creation of semantic meaning. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics, yet it disregards syntactic constraints when generating word suggestions. We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an activity potential, which is used to create detailed simulations. These simulations confirm that particle orientation significantly affects their collective motion direction. This research provides insights into the complex behavior of active colloidal molecules, potentially expanding their use in biomedical applications. It also identifies areas where further study is required to fully understand their functionality. This study was supported by funding from the Singapore Ministry of Education and the National University of Singapore. It appears in Volume 122 of Physical Review Letters, published in 2023. 

Keywords: Active Colloidal Particles, Activity Gradients, Chemotaxis, Antichemotaxis, Nanoscale Robotics.

The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparison with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in different configurations, and the second explores flow and transport through a large stochastically generated network of 257 fractures. Our model demonstrates satisfactory results, and the proposed framework is deemed suitable for simulating single-phase flow in complex fractured reservoirs. Additionally, it can be expanded to tackle multiple phase flow and transport applications. Our code is a free resource, accessible through https://github.com/numsim2dfm/frt_mfd.
