Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation profiles.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

Ultimately, we conclude that stars exhibiting anti-solar differential rotation can only support magnetic cycles under highly localized $\alpha$-effect dynamos, whereas hybrid models featuring both kinematic and flux-transport dynamos can experience local polarity reversals at specific latitudes. These findings underscore the complexities of understanding solar and stellar magnetic dynamics and the need for further observational evidence. Additionally, we suggest that stars with undetermined rotation profiles should be subjected to detailed stellar activity observations for a more precise understanding of their rotation and magnetic behavior. Additionally, we outline the necessary steps to study the relationship between the shape of the rotation profile and the behavior of the magnetic field. Lastly, we highlight the potential implications of our research on early search strategies for extraterrestrial life and the detection of solar types and slow rotators in the search for artifacts. Deep multimodal learning using K-fan deep Boltzmann machines offers a novel approach to combine multiple input sources. This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine lies in its inability to handle complex tasks effectively, lack of clear theoretical foundations, and limited capacity to handle multiple input modalities. Our study develops a deep K-fan model consisting of multiple layers to tackle complex tasks with multiple input sources. The proposed deep model uses K-fan units with independent visible layers for different input sources and shares a common hidden layer across all units in a single layer or across multiple layers in a deep model. The model is initially applied to a synthetic dataset and later to a real-world video classification dataset. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the deep model outperforming standard two-fan deep models. The code for the model is available online at https://github.com/SaharNassar/Deep-K-fan-models. The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to the hidden nature of race conditions, which can evade detection by these tests. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own thread activation policies, including the handling of spurious wake-ups triggered by condition variables. By specifying (i) when operations are allowed, (ii) which thread operations are mutually independent, and (iii) when operations can co-occur, users can define their own customized thread activation policies. Additionally, users can define custom wake-up policies by specifying when wait operations, such as those involving semaphores or condition variables, are permitted. A new enqueue thread operation was introduced, which allows users to define custom wake-up policies, such as first-in, first-out, last-in, first-out, and arbitrary order, and so forth. The McMini model checker's efficiency was validated through its correct and efficient operation in testing traditional multi-threaded constructs like mutexes, semaphores, and reader-writer operations. Furthermore, its extensibility was evaluated using novel, useful thread operation paradigms such as readers and two writers, demonstrating an up to fivefold reduction in the code required to model check these constructs compared to traditional approaches. Finally, the model checker's versatility was assessed using a program that illustrated how to correctly implement the reader-writer synchronization technique using thread-local arrays and custom wake-up policies. The results showed that McMini was capable of validating the correctness of this program, which it did using only 42 lines of model checking code. The model checker's efficiency, extensibility, and versatility highlight the benefits of using a programmable DPOR-based model checker to validate the correctness of multi-threaded programs. The model checker's source code is publicly available at https://mcmini.github.io/. The McMini model checker is now capable of supporting a wide range of thread operation paradigms not initially contemplated during its original design. The success of McMini in validating novel multi-threaded operation paradigms serves as evidence that it is a versatile tool that can be used in a wide range of applications beyond its initial scope. The globally predominant messaging app, WhatsApp, boasts a distinct characteristic 
in its closed nature and user-friendly capabilities of transferring multimedia and
large-scale information sharing to groups, which often facilitates the rapid spread 
of anonymous, encrypted messages. However, the direct delivery of messages to user 
phones enabled by WhatsApp, although personal and immediate, can be exploited to 
circulate baseless rumors and fuel misinformation campaigns. Recent elections in 
Brazil and India are notable examples of such abuse, which have led WhatsApp to 
initiate countermeasures like limiting forwarded messages to a single recipient. 
Despite this effort, the success of these measures remains uncertain. In our study, 
we utilize an epidemiological model coupled with real data from WhatsApp in Brazil, 
India, and Indonesia to investigate the impact of limiting features that contribute 
to rapid information dissemination. Our analysis reveals that current WhatsApp 
restrictions can delay the spread of information but are ultimately insufficient to 
halt the dissemination of highly viral misinformation campaigns within public groups. 
Conversely, removing features that enable group creation or massive message sending 
to groups would significantly mitigate the spread of such malware. We also find that 
indicating sent messages with a logo or applying reverse image search to detect 
hoaxes could be effective in slowing down misinformation spread. Our findings are 
first-order, as they align with real-world scenarios, and can guide the design of 
message delivery systems to prevent the abuse of anonymous, immediate messaging. 
Furthermore, our analysis on Indonesia reveals that the spread of information 
follows a predictable pattern in response to certain group features. We discovered 
stabilizing patterns in message circulation among groups in Brazil and India, 
although these were less pronounced. We also explore the potential abuse of 
WhatsApp links and voice messages, as well as unsend features, drawing analogies to 
unprecedented events and societal trends in Indonesia. Our model is versatile and 
can be utilized to investigate various scenarios and design experiments to prevent 
misinformation dissemination. It is notable that our analysis on Brazil, India, and 
Indonesia was conducted before WhatsApp initiated its recent efforts to counter 
misinformation. We provide regular updates on WhatsApp's current countermeasures 
and the latest information on real user behavior in these countries. We also 
maintain an online repository where the source code and data for our study are 
publicly available. As WhatsApp continues to initiate new countermeasures, such as 
labelling political messages in Brazil and temporarily assigning names to 
messages, we examine their success in reducing misinformation

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which describes the approximate proportions of individuals within the population carrying a specific number of genetic defects by time $t$. The difficulty in solving this frequency spectrum analytically motivates the introduction of two simplified models: one where new individuals are assigned genetic types randomly, and another where existing individuals experience continuous genetic evolution. By investigating these models, we establish a formula for the frequency spectrum in the first model and demonstrate that it converges to a frequency spectrum in the second model as time progresses, which in turn converges to a frequency spectrum from a related Wright-Fisher model after further time scaling. Ultimately, all of these frequency spectra are shown to converge to a frequency spectrum in a related Kingman's model. The models and results have significant implications in understanding the approximate composition of a general branching population, and the connection to a related Kingman's model. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access task using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset and outperformed existing systems, specifically those utilizing traditional activation functions and multi-task learning approaches. Our experimental findings highlight the significance of utilizing a responsive, feature-sensitive activation function in spoofing countermeasure systems. Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and ensuring the scalars remain heavy compared to the Hubble scale to facilitate single-field inflation.  Additionally, supergravity predicts several non-renormalizable interactions, rendering it an effective field theory that remains valid up to a specific cutoff energy scale, and thus necessitates a re-examination of the scalar potentials and field dynamics to achieve self-consistency at the quantum level. Furthermore, by incorporating the unique quantum gravity predictions, this research demonstrates how the properties of these fields can be accurately determined at the quantum level, and subsequently translates these findings into the distinct predictions for the primordial spectrum and non-Gaussianity in the cosmic microwave background for these supergravity inspired inflation models. In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - in markets with both types of traders, CTA profitability and activity actually increased. Consequently, a positive symbiotic relationship between these traders may be more likely than initially assumed. In order to further understand this phenomenon, a computer program was developed to analyze various trading methodologies used by both the CTA and SRT. It was found that both types of traders employ distinct approaches to trading, leading to a multi-dimensional trading environment with interdependent strategies. In particular, it was observed that an SRT's success depends on the behavior of a particular CTA strategy, while an SRT's own trading methods have a negative impact on a particular CTA strategy's profitability. The study's results also revealed that an SRT's trading actions are closely linked to those of a particular CTA strategy, while an SRT may even imitate some of the CTA's practices. It was further found that an SRT's performance in a artificial market model is comparable to that of a purely technical trading approach. In conclusion, it appears that an SRT's trading actions are multifaceted and influenced by various factors, while their relationship with a CTA is one of mutual interdependence. Furthermore, it seems that an SRT may be replicating some of the CTA's behaviors in their trading practices. As a result, it is difficult to conclude that an SRT's existence harms a CTA for financial gain. Rather, it is possible that an SRT is merely emulating the behaviors of a competent CTA. Consequently, it may be more accurate to describe the dynamic between an SRT and a CTA as a beneficial and interconnected relationship. In order to further explore this hypothesis, the research recommends examining the trading practices of both types of advisors in actual markets to establish whether their behaviors are similarly interconnected. Additionally, it may be worthwhile to apply the model used in this study to analyze the relationships between different trading strategies in actual markets.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerging from unseen data patterns on various devices challenge this methodology as they are not accessible to the central server or fellow users. In this paper, a unified system called Zero-Shot Federated Learning is proposed to address this issue by introducing a data-less and computation-less technique for federated learning. This system is comprised of two distinct processes: the static part, involving clustering users and categorizing data, and the dynamic part, involving dynamic updates of the model and cluster assignments. Moreover, to tackle the issue of uneven data distributions across users, a Random Walk layer is suggested to guarantee fair participation of all users in the learning process. Experimental results from three different datasets (SCUT-summ-1, SCUT-summ-2, and VGGSound) have shown that the proposed system outperforms traditional federated learning and deep clustering methods under a federated learning framework. The code for this research can be accessed at https://github.com/whs615/Zero-Shot-FL. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information. Our findings imply that local news can play a significant role in informing the public about crucial issues like public health, and its coverage can be influenced by various contextual factors. Given the current decline of local news, our research also highlights the essential function of these outlets in providing citizens with accurate information. The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned. By comparing this system to other advanced machine learning methods, we found that it was uniquely capable of generalizing counting rules in a way that's similar to human children' exceptional learning abilities. Our study suggests that the emergence of new abilities in AIs can be a valuable tool for better understanding the cognitive development in humans. You can find the source code for this research at https://github.com/whiteagnees/esbn_counting. Additionally, the trained ESBN models are available for download at https://idle-ml-data.s3.amazonaws.com/esbn_counting.zip. Our results are mirrored on Github at https://github.com/whiteagnees/esbn_counting_results. We have also made available a demo where you can interact with our ESBN models and see the amazing generalization abilities for yourself. You can access the demo at https://idle-ml.github.io/esbn-demo/. We hope that our study and demo will contribute to a deeper understanding of the emergence of new abilities in AIs and the fascinating learning abilities of human children. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming operations and control the amount of main memory used efficiently. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different filter, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter. Our research involves developing a new compact approximate membership filter called the Xor filter, which is inspired by this concept. Our evaluations demonstrate that Xor filters surpass both Bloom and cuckoo filters in both speed and storage efficiency. To our knowledge, Xor filters are the first filters to achieve equal performance in both aspects. Our experiments also show the benefits of combining Xor filters with hierarchical aggregation of smaller filters to handle larger datasets efficiently. A significant outcome of our findings is that approximate membership filters are now suitable for use cases that previously required exact membership filters. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski existence theorem, Demazure-Mumford theorem, and the Cho-Young theorem within the language of algebraic geometry, showcasing the additive metric on the cone of divisor classes or linear systems on a divisor class. Furthermore, we discuss the nondegenerateness in combination with a new concept involving hypersection indices and establish interesting properties for geometrically fibered projective varieties. Our work is motivated by the relationships between convex geometry, algebraic geometry, and transverse singularities. These relationships are particularly evident in the examples of hypersurfaces, frequently referenced in the text. We expect our investigations to yield significant insights into the global structure of the convergence locus of many well-known hypersurfaces, such as the quartic and the cubic, although we only provide a preview of such conclusions in the concluding section. Specifically, our studies suggest the existence of rationally connected varieties with the property that their smooth compactifications do not contain algebraic torus factors and have a topologically connected threshold locus. A comprehensive overview of the completed research, along with additional details, is provided in the accompanying notes. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and precludes data exposure. Importantly, it achieves performance comparable to conventional FL methods, including LGKD and RRSL, while maintaining a significant improvement in privacy protection. Notably, the source code for this research is publicly accessible on https://github.com/jbunetti/FLVoogd. Experimental results show that FLVoogd successfully isolates malicious clients and achieves a data use percentage exceeding 98% despite being subject to intense attacks (up to 20% of malicious participants). Moreover, it significantly reduces the number of required communication rounds by 4.5 to 5.5 times compared to state-of-the-art approaches while maintaining comparable test accuracy. This is particularly evident in the CIFAR10 benchmark, where FLVoogd outperforms the closest competitor (RRSL) by enhancing test accuracy and reducing the number of communication rounds. Additionally, FLVoogd efficiently prevents data exposure, as shown by its 4.5 to 5.5 times improvement in the data use percentage compared to RRSL and a 6.2 to 7.2 times improvement in the weight distribution. This is particularly evident in the CIFAR10 benchmark, where FLVoogd outperforms the closest competitor (RRSL) by reducing the standard deviation of the weight distribution and the data exposure percentage. Lastly, FLVoogd successfully balances this trade-off in datasets with varying sizes, as exemplified by its 2.8 to 4.8 times improvement in the data use percentage and 1.4 to 2.8 times improvement in the weight distribution standard deviation in the miniImageNet dataset. Ultimately, FLVoogd offers a robust and efficient FL method that effectively blocks malicious clients, maintains user anonymity, and achieves a robust model with a minimal number of communication rounds. This chapter examines the advancements and difficulties in the production and identification of deepfakes, and also explores the potential solutions to improve the resilience of deepfake detection for a broad range of media, such as real-world images and videos. Please note that this chapter does not represent an exhaustive literature review on the topic but rather offers our personal insights and perspectives.

Compared to the current state-of-the-art models, our approach demonstrates superior performance on a variety of public datasets. 

In addition to contribution, we also discuss the limitations of existing deepfake detection methods and possible future research directions on robust deepfake detection from an unsupervised and domain-adversarial perspective. Also, we explore other potential applications of deepfake technology, such as the integration of deepfake into various cutting-edge technologies and deepfake-related ethical considerations. 

In the end, we summarize the key points and provide our thoughts on the topic.

Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns of binary vectors, an ability similar to that of symmetric Hopfield networks for spatial patterns. Furthermore, our study reveals the model's capability to efficiently acquire sequences of binary images and generate neural spike-train data. Our model adheres to spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) principles, offering a theoretical framework for the systematic design of biological neural networks capable of long-term, robust sequence storage. The model's biological plausibility is further demonstrated by our experiments, which showed that even with limited systematic learning, the model could effectively retrieve sequences from noisy spike-train data, exhibiting a high degree of similarity with the original binary images. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those specifically designed for OCR revealed a significant disparity in performance for both tasks.

The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and available resources. Moreover, industrial systems may exhibit multiple failure patterns, and identifying the primary cause is essential. This work aims to develop an adaptive monitoring system capable of handling high-dimensional data in resource-scarce environments where various potential failures may occur. Our proposed solution incorporates the Shiryaev-Roberts method for change detection and an approach based on Mahalanobis Distance to isolate the root cause of an alteration. Through an analysis of its theoretical and practical aspects, along with simulations and real-world case studies, we demonstrate that our solution can provide accurate results with minimal computational requirements. Furthermore, we explore the trade-offs between accuracy and computational complexity. Our change detection approach shows significant efficiency improvements, while our CFI strategy exhibits high isolation accuracy even in resource-constrained environments. Notably, our monitor's performance can be further enhanced through data reduction techniques at the cost of increased computational complexity. We highlight that our isolation performance may decline in scenarios with very limited data availability but demonstrate through case studies that this drawback can be overcome through simple data augmentation approaches, resulting in our method being applicable to a broad range of real-world applications. Our source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jb-learn/APS-CDI. Experimental data is available on GitHub. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively and efficiently training pruned models. Our proposed algorithm, ClickTrain, addresses this gap by introducing a innovative, fine-grained pruning approach that preserves the original model architecture during training. The process enhances the accuracy of pruning models through a refinement process, where sub-layer precision is applied to convolutional operations. The key benefits of ClickTrain are threefold: it achieves nearly native model accuracy in inference mode, requires significantly fewer resources for computing parameters, and facilitates easy implementation into existing CNN frameworks. The empirical evaluation demonstrates that ClickTrain outperforms state-of-the-art methods in nearly all evaluation metrics. Moreover, the framework exhibits a striking balance between model size and inference speed, making it an ideal solution for efficient end-to-end pruning model training. The code for this research is openly accessible on GitHub. \\

Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by an extremely vast number of states and actions, as well as a difficult-to-compute transition matrix. To resolve these challenges, we develop an algorithm that combines policy iteration with subgradient ascent. We show that this approach allows the CMDP to converge to a solution at a rate proportional to $O(\log(T)/\sqrt{T})$, where T represents the number of iterations, provided that a specific condition is met. This method also offers an efficient way to reduce the dimensionality of the CMDP by exploiting its structural properties when applicable. We successfully apply our algorithm to critical problems with such a structure: multi-product inventory control and multi-class queue management, achieving results superior to state-of-art methods. Experimental analysis further confirms the efficacy of our approach. It is worth noting that while our algorithm shows improved performance over existing methods, it has a somewhat higher computational complexity. However, we argue that the added computational efficiency due to reduced dimensionality outweighs this disadvantage. We make our implemented code available at https://github.com/nicolasbousquet/PrimalDualCMDP. Additionally, we document our techniques in the tutorial "Towards optimal operating policies in sequential decision making", available at https://nbviewer.jupyter.org/ url=https://nbviewer.jupyter.org/urls/sharing.cmg.co/7f0d7b9c/towardsoptimaloperatingpolicies.ipnb. The duality is established by identifying the black hole's BPS states with momentum states in the superconformal quantum mechanics. Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic model. To address these shortcomings, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the Hamiltonian Policy. In doing so, our novel method has numerous benefits, primarily in reducing the gap between the approximated posterior and optimal policy distribution. Furthermore, our approach optimizes exploration within action spaces by targeting areas with higher expected returns. To achieve this, a new leapfrog operator has been developed for simulating Hamiltonian dynamics. Furthermore, our approach enables the efficient incorporation of large prior distributions in action spaces, thereby enhancing local and global policy exploration. Through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments, our results demonstrate that the HP-HMC method achieves better performance and faster convergence in comparison to standard actor-critic models. Notably, our numerical tests have shown that the HP-HMC method leads to an average performance improvement of 10-50% over the baseline actor-critic model. A comprehensive open-source implementation of the proposed method is available at https://github.com/yusongyang/hp-hmc.html. This repository includes the necessary code for reproducing the presented results. Additionally, an interactive Jupyter notebook has been created for educating students on the HP-HMC framework through a simple grid world example. The notebook can be accessed at https://github.com/yusongyang/learnrobotics.html. In the future, we aim to extend our approach to enable the learning of discrete control policies. Additionally, we are currently developing methods for applying the HP-HMC framework in online reinforcement learning settings. These efforts are expected to be documented in future articles. To facilitate research in this area, our code includes a range of useful tools and examples for online reinforcement learning, such as the implementation of standard actor-critic models, in addition to the HP-HMC framework. These examples include simple grid world scenarios with moving obstacles, as well as more complex robotic arm control tasks. As a result, researchers can leverage our code by selecting the training options to suit their specific needs, including the choice of using or omitting Hamiltonian dynamics. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, as often occurs in densely vegetated areas, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to provide accurate map data. A novel method has been developed to enable a mobile robot to efficiently move through areas with heavy vegetation where normal sensing methods are less effective. Our solution involves creating a layered control system that utilizes sonar sensors to facilitate accurate navigation in real-time, especially in environments where vision and infrared sensing capabilities are limited. The system leverages a modified sonar-based controller to overcome obstacles and enable a mobile robot to move accurately in areas with or without vision, including scenarios involving multiple intersecting paths and changing environments. The integration of a global planner allows the robot to optimize its path and adapt to new situations, while an error compensation module ensures a smoother and more efficient navigation experience. The system's performance in a simulated environment has been demonstrated to be comparable to that of an optocoupler, and with the advancement of affordable and high-resolution sonar technologies, this method provides an affordable and effective solution for mobile robots to navigate a variety of environments. The system design provides the flexibility to accommodate a wide range of sensing technologies and can be widely adopted in navigation systems for mobile robots. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characterization utilizing its reflectance spectrum between 0.8-2.4 $\mu m$, particularly in the unexplored 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$ range, as we attempt to identify the spectral absorption features that correspond to its icy composition. Our findings indicate the presence of crystalline water ice, coinciding with existing observations. Nonetheless, using simple models consisting of intimate water ice mixtures, we fail to attain a comprehensive match of absorption bands, especially considering the spectral continuum, at the wavelengths of 1.5 and 2.0 $\mu m$. This could be resolved by accounting for both crystalline and amorphous water ice, as well as taking into account the influence of sub-micron grain sizes. Our estimates of albedo at 550 $\mu m$ narrows the range of existing measurements, as reported by three observations. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise the pessimism degree without manual adjustment. By developing a credible set with an optimistically bounded Q-function boundary, the need for additional pessimism parameter tuning is eliminated. Our general Bayesian learning method can accommodate a range of models, including Bayesian linear and neural network models. Additionally, a variational inference algorithm is developed to efficiently generate the optimised dynamic treatment regimes from the credible set. The theoretical soundness and performance of our approach in realistic scenarios are supported by both controlled numerical studies and a case study using electronic health records. The study shows that our approach produces highly competitive results with state-of-the-art methods. The authors provide an open-source implementation of their solution, including data and code, on public repositories. Specifically, the code is shared on GitHub and the data on MIRA, both under public licences. The repository is available at the link: https://github.com/woc2004/optim_pessimism_Bayes_Learning. The dataset can be found at the link: https://cuiadlab.mira.es/system/files/projects/woc2004_optim_pessimism_Bayes_Learning.zip.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, and further distinguishes between materials with unique attenuation characteristics. In support of this model, the proposed iterative algorithm has been mathematically justified and verified with numerical reconstructions of data collected from a test setup. The outcomes display the reconstructor's ability to produce high-quality images with reduced noise and accurate differentiation of various materials. Moreover, the model parameters can be adjusted to prioritize either system denoising or polyenergetic correction. These results have also been compared to recently published methods, and the reconstruction results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed model. Ultimately, the study showcases the potential of the proposed model in achieving superior image quality through polyenergetic correction and sensor denoising. Additionally, the study highlights the capabilities and limitations of the model in accurately distinguishing between materials with similar attenuation characteristics. These findings are expected to extend the applications of CT into fields such as multi-phase medical image analysis and various industrial inspection techniques. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for line segmentation. Thorough evaluation and analysis affirm the efficacy of the proposed solution. Notably, using the generated data, the error rate for the UliNet model decreased by 25%, while also surpassing existing handwritten digit recognition benchmarks. Moreover, this study's solution won the 2020 SHTask challenge in handwritten text recognition, thereby setting a new standard for low-resource HTR. The proposed program structure and the associated code are made available for the community to build upon. Additionally, the generated datasets will be made accessible under a free license. Furthermore, the evaluation results, including the best-performing model configurations, are provided to guarantee reproducibility of the findings. To ensure generalizability, the study includes a significant number of training data, thereby allowing the program to learn from the available data without the need for line-level annotations. Moreover, the study validates the efficacy of the proposed solution by conducting ablation studies and analyzing the generated datasets through t-SNE and other metrics. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach Tries memory management and memory access simultaneously, thereby yielding a notable performance boost in speed.  Our framework's ease of use is further illustrated through examples of successful applications using DynaSOAr, including real-world programs of significant complexity.  Our experiments demonstrate that DynaSOAr's atomic approach to memory allocation and memory access yields a significant performance boost in speed, specifically up to 30% improvement over leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators for SMMO applications.  Additionally, DynaSOAr offers improved memory efficiency, thereby increasing the average runtime performance of the tested applications by up to 15%.  Our research includes an in-depth analysis of the atomic approach for simultaneous memory allocation and memory access in DynaSOAr, as well as the performance characteristics of this framework.  Our findings indicate that DynaSOAr not only offers a notable performance boost in speed but also improves memory efficiency, thereby making it an efficient solution for parallelizing SMMO applications on SIMD devices.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's ease of use is demonstrated through examples of successful applications, highlighting the effectiveness of object-oriented programming with single-method and multiple-objects structures for high-speed GPU programming.  Our research includes a detailed comparison of DynaSOAr with leading state-of-the-and GPU memory allocators through benchmark experiments, specifically focusing on real-world applications of varying complexity.  Our findings indicate that DynaSOAr yields a significant performance boost in speed

In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models representing the unknown environment with confidence intervals on key variables. Focusing on the 'Maximum Marginal Probability' (MaMo) problem – the generalization of the Maximum Probability of Detection in classification tasks – our approach transforms MaMo into a more manageable problem within the realm of probabilistic circuits. Utilizing an efficient simplification, we reduce MaMo over a credal Bayesian network to a convex optimization problem involving the minimax of a convex-concave function, thereby providing robustness guarantees for Bayesian network quantification. Experimental results showcasing the efficiency of this approach and its order-of-magnitude improvement compared to existing methods are presented. Furthermore, the study includes a theoretical analysis probing the trade-offs between problem assumptions and performance guarantees. Our findings are substantiated by practical applications in intrusion detection and coverage path planning. A Python package enabling the computation of MaMo values for credal Bayesian networks and Bayesian networks is also made available. Additionally, the corresponding PC-MaMo solver is offered as an open-source tool. Lastly, a circuit generator for the BN-MaMo problem is presented as an open-source tool. Due to space constraints, this material is presented in an appendix. Please see the supplementary materials for more information. A publicly accessible Python package containing the code for these resources can be found at https://github.com/jose-angel/robust_bayes.

The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Our analysis focuses on the 4$d$ shell of nickel and demonstrates that subtle variations in the 4$d$ shell electronic structure can be resolved through measurements of the edge-up energy. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The proposed temperature sensor outperforms several state-of-the-art designs in terms of resolution, inaccuracy, and power efficiency while providing a highly efficient area usage. With its compact design and capability for dynamic voltage and temperature monitoring, this temperature sensor is well-suited for use in temperature-aware biomedical applications and deep sub-micron digital microcontrol unit (DMCU) systems. Moreover, the sensor can be utilized as a temperature reference for various biomedical applications and DMCUs, eliminating the need for an external temperature compensation mechanism. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired form of entangled states. The feasibility of this approach is demonstrated by preparing entangled states of polarized photons and verifying their properties through experiments and theoretical calculations, which are concurrently performed. In particular, a demonstrated experiment achieved an entanglement figure of merit greater than 0.5, indicating a entanglement figure of 0.52. This method not only enables the first heralded preparation of polarization entanglement but also provides a versatile tool for generating various complex quantum states, making it an essential component for applications in quantum information science and technologies. By combining this method with current technology, it is feasible to achieve an entanglement figure of 0.9 within reach in near-future experiments. Additionally, this approach offers an advantage over other available methods by providing enhanced stability against environmental perturbations, as demonstrated through theoretical calculations. In particular, it is anticipated that entanglement figures above 0.9 could be achieved through technical improvements involving the careful selection of quantum memory materials. The entanglement properties of the proposed approach are thoroughly analyzed using metrics such as the entanglement figure of merit and the convergence half-time, which are established as important indicators of entanglement quality. It is anticipated that this research will contribute to various applications of quantum entanglement and enable the development of numerous quantum information technologies. The proposed strategy may also contribute to the creation of quantum clock networks, which rely on entangled states to synchronize clocks over long distances. This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log ε^(-1)) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for points in 1-dimension, proving it to be tight. For sequences of points in R^d, the authors present algorithms under the L_2 norm that achieve previously known competitive ratios but allow for Steiner points to be added to substantially improve the competitive ratio in terms of ε. However, the authors also prove that eliminating the dependence on n in dimensions d ≥ 2 is not possible, while providing improved lower bounds under the L_1 norm: Ω(ε^(-2)/log ε^(-1)) in the plane and Ω(ε^(-d)) in R^d for d≥3. This lower bound is currently the best known for the plane, while in higher dimensions the previous result could be improved upon by simply applying a rounding technique to the solution. Additionally, the authors propose an online algorithm for sequences of points in R^d that achieves a competitive ratio of O(ε^(-d/2)) under the L_2 norm, and prove that its competitive ratio could be as high as O(ε^(-d/2) log ε^(-1)) in the plane if the points lie near the x-axis. Finally, the authors present an online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for sequences of points in R^d that achieves a competitive ratio of O(ε^(-d/2) / (log(1/ε))^(d+1)), and show that its competitive ratio could be as high as O(ε^(-d/2) / (log(1/ε))^(d+2)) in the plane if the points lie near the x-axis. These algorithms feature Steiner points that significantly improve the competitive ratio in terms of ε, while also introducing new geometric concepts: shape spanners and shape Steiner points. The authors conclude by applying these concepts to improve the competitive ratio in terms of ε for achieving online Euclidean b-spansners under the L_2 norm. This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment metrics, such as accuracy or F-score, our approach delivers results equivalent to GIZA++ when trained on a dataset 22 times smaller. Crucially, the method's domain-agnostic training capabilities enable 'on-the-fly' application on any new pair of sentences without requiring extensive retraining. We also highlight external sources of bilingual information that can augment our approach and enhance its quality. We visually illustrate the benefits of our alignment model through'sentence embeddings', which show the model capturing complex and meaningful structures in the bilingual space. We openly provide the code for this research through a link. Additionally, we propose an improved validation strategy to evaluate word-alignment models in a more rigorous manner. We demonstrate using our alignment model to achieve improvements in existing sentence embedding benchmarks, such as IEMB. We further show the benefits of our alignment model in two real-world NLP tasks: bilingual sentence similarity and zero-shot translation. Leveraging the 'on-the-fly' capabilities, we report performance gains in these tasks by outperforming the current state-of-the-art models. To showcase the efficacy of our alignment model in more nuanced scenarios, we also provide a detailed analysis using t-SNE in Figure 10 in the main paper. We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures. Furthermore, we outline a corresponding dual algorithm based on the Fischer-Burmeister function, showing that both the primal and dual algorithms converge to the solution of the Nash equilibrium. The convergence speed can be analyzed using the Lipschitz constant of the Nash equilibrium map, and under certain conditions, can also be determined by the Lipschitz constant of the mixed strategies. Numerical tests are performed to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm. In particular, it is demonstrated that, in comparison to existing methods, our algorithm can achieve improved computational efficiency when dealing with large-scale nonlinear matrix factorization problems and Stackelberg game problems in power management. The code for these experiments is available at https://github.com/ccaguirre/NashEquilibrium. The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting primordial black holes using PopSyCLE, we modified the code to account for a dark matter halo composition consisting of these hypothetical black holes. Our analysis involves examining the predicted number of microlensing events that could be observed in a specific astronomical survey, taking into account factors such as the ages and light produced by stars in the galaxy in question. This analysis reveals that while running the PopSyCLE code, we encountered an unexpected issue related to the use of units, which we describe in the following solution. Our study indicates that while current astronomical surveys show no signs of the required gravitational microlensing evidence for primordial black holes consistent with existing data, they do not rule out this possibility entirely. Ultimately, future surveys may be able to confirm or refute the idea that primordial black holes comprise the dark matter in our universe. To facilitate this evaluation, we made available a user-friendly web application where researchers can input their own assumptions about the properties of these early universe black holes and see how it affects the predicted number of detectable microlensing signals. Our study also reveals an intriguing connection between the hypothetical dark matter composed of primordial black holes and the observed distribution of nearby stars, which may hold additional insights into this theoretical astrophysical phenomenon. In addition, we explored an alternative approach using PopSyCLE to study the occurrence of specific star-related signals that could serve as evidence for early universe black holes, which may provide further signs of their existence. To facilitate this evaluation, we developed a companion tool where users can modify various assumptions about the early universe and see how it affects the predicted number of relevant star-related signals. Our study used specific astronomical data, but our approach is designed to be adaptable to other types of data, which may provide further insights into the theoretical early universe black holes. To make our research more accessible, we built a public web-page where users can explore our findings and reproduce our analysis. We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied across various parameter values, from closed shapes with a parameter value of $0.5$ to rod-like shapes with a parameter value of $0.8$, and under these conditions, the systems displayed both liquid crystalline and crystalline configurations. In addition to these configurations, we observed an isolated particle-like phase and a gaseous phase consisting of non-touching molecules, and the systems' behaviors were influenced by the shape modulation in the molecules through the application of parameter $d$. The systems' thermodynamic characteristics were unaffected by the modulation in the enthalpy and entropy of the molecules, but did result in the alteration of the compressibility of the systems in certain parameter value ranges, particularly in the gaseous phase and a second order phase transition in the systems. Moreover, we verified that the systems exhibiting liquid crystalline phases were susceptible to nematic and smectic phase formations, and noted that certain systems were trapped in metastable states. A comprehensive analysis of the systems' compressibility was conducted, and we compared our simulation results with the results of previous research on similar systems consisting of prolate ellipsoids, as well as other systems consisting of soft wedges. Finally, we studied the systems' behavior in confinement by applying pressure in the simulations and examining the changes in the systems' configurations in narrow containers. These changes led to the alteration of the systems' compressibility and the formation of new configurations in the systems. All of these results provide insights into the systems consisting of hard wedge-shaped molecules and demonstrate the possibility of designing new materials with these unique molecular shapes. Moreover, we observed that the systems consisting of hard wedge-shaped molecules displayed different configurations at high pressures than systems consisting of soft wedge-shaped molecules, and were also different from systems consisting of prolate ellipsoids under these same conditions. Additionally, we verified that certain systems consisting of hard wedge-shaped molecules were trapped in metastable states, which were different from systems consisting of soft wedge-shaped molecules, and noted that systems consisting of hard wedge-shaped molecules displayed higher enthalpy values than systems consisting of soft wedge-shaped molecules. These findings also allow for the design of new materials with unique high-pressure configurations that can be achieved through the utilization of wedge-shaped molecules

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. These novel recurrence operators enable the efficient computation of zonal functions on the sphere with a single iteration step. The paper also presents a shorthanded form of the recurrence, expressed in terms of the conventional differential operator, and verifies the applicability of the recurrence to stochastic random fields on the sphere. The provided examples illustrate the accelerated computation of the field's mean squared value and its scaling behavior under a sphere volume change. The approach has been implemented in the R package SphereRecurrences. The necessary nonstandard mathematical operations have been explained in detail to facilitate the implementation. The operators can also be extended to maintain (strict) positive definiteness in functions that are not necessarily zonal. The theoretical findings can be extended to other spaces, such as the torus and the hyperball, and the recruited operators will likely have applications in other domains of specialized functions. The approach has been tested in examples involving Bessel functions and the Mat\'ern kernel. The integration of the spherical recurrence operators into CRAN is planned. The provided R code in SphereRecurrences generates synthetic data, demonstrates the accelerated computation of the field's mean squared value and its scaling behavior under a sphere volume change, and presents a comparative analysis of the computation times for different methods. The employed strategy has been tested on data from the NetCDF-CF standard and shown to be compatible with packages such as climatR and geoExSe. The approaches can also be used to develop new Gaussian process regression methods with a single iteration step, and the theoretical findings may contribute to the development of new non-stationary spatial models. The zonal functions can be efficiently computed using the GPC R package and the Cholesky matrix from spSvd, leading to significant time savings for spatial statistics computations. The presented recurrence relations provide a compact alternative to computing zonal functions

A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a means to detect this scattered light; and a detector that can resolve spatial information. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for delicate biological specimens or sensitive samples due to the inadequacy of available light-detecting capabilities and potential harm from light interaction. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a quantum imaging protocol that achieves all this by leveraging the unique properties of a Michelson interferometer and combining it with the advanced functionality of a single-pixel camera. By utilizing undetected photons in the scheme, our method enables interaction-free imaging that allows for coherent light interaction with the subject while minimizing detected photons. This breakthrough incorporates various advanced techniques such as phase retrieval, Mueller imaging, and Hadamard transform to maintain the highest possible signal-to-noise ratio. As a demonstration of its capabilities, we have successfully reconstructed detailed images of a USA one-dollar coin and a biological sample with integrated fluorescent markers, all through a process that requires no special lighting. The developed scheme now offers a versatile and versatile means of quantum imaging that could soon contribute significantly to various applications across biological, medical, and military domains. Additionally, we have explored the fundamental limitations of our imaging protocol and discovered that it is subject to a quantum imaging limit that is dictated by the inherent incoherence of most subjects, despite having the potential to reach a superior incoherence-limited imaging performance if paired with a highly coherent light source. This study paves the way for further research on the Coherent Imaging of Objects (CIO). Lastly, we have devised a novel strategy to surpass the conventional Rayleigh limit through the clever manipulation of Michelson interferometry and the incorporation of an extra beam splitter, thereby enabling the reconstruction of detailed images even when only a small amount of light is scattered off the subject of interest. This innovation has the potential to greatly expand the scope of single-pixel imaging. To verify the efficacy of our methods, we have thoroughly performed and presented the results of numerous rigorous experiments and analyzed the results with simple, clear interpretations. To sum up, we have now have available a reliable and versatile means of quantum imaging that allows for delicate interactions with the subject while minimizing harm from photons, and this imaging method also possesses the potential to greatly surpass the conventional imaging performance by leveraging the advanced functionality of a single-pixel camera, undetected photons, and a Michelson interferometer. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The stick-slip regime is characterized by a "leverage window" where stress peaks due to the placement of a border on a particular asperity. The persistence of the stationary regime over long periods indicates a substantial energy barrier that must be overcome for the foam's dynamics to progress. The presence of such an energy barrier is analogous to that observed in amorphous glasses and may provide insights into understanding it through the use of a particle or grain model. The findings of this study, obtained in a regime where surface slippage prevails, can also be used to refine existing models for liquid slip. Additionally, our research provides new perspectives on the dynamics of liquid foams and may shed light on the flow of foams over rough surfaces. Lastly, we explored the possibility of observing dynamic changes between the different friction modes by changing the surface roughness or the curvature of Plateau borders. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized by Alahmadi et al. in 2015, and it follows logically that quartic graphs should be the subject of characterization next. Conversely, it is also proven that every accordion graph possesses the PH-property. Ultimately, it is shown that quartic graphs that possess the PH-property are either isomorphic to an accordion graph or a quartic circulant graph under specific cyclic groups. This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, our research highlights the significance of incorporating a momentum encoder, employing multi-crop training, and using small patch sizes when utilizing ViTs. Building upon these insights, we developed the DINO self-supervised method, a form of self-distillation without the need for labelled data, and demonstrated its effectiveness by achieving an 80.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when evaluating ViT-Base linearly. Our work does not address the issue of object classification, but rather focuses on the properties of visual representations, in order to contribute to the ongoing debate on the necessity of supervision in ViT and the potential of self-supervised methods to surpass labelled data approaches. The proposed self-supervised method now holds the record for the highest linear evaluation accuracy on ImageNet for ViT-Base and ViT-Large. Importantly, it also surpasses the state-of-the-art ranking of convnets and supervised ViTs when evaluating these models under a robustness metric. Therefore, we believe that self-supervised ViTs may be more resilient to adversarial attacks than models trained with labelled data. A comprehensive comparison of convnets, supervised ViTs, and self-supervised ViTs is provided on our website. This research was funded by the ERC Grant Signer. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key capability is to guide the diffusion latent space toward specific semantic targets, enabling synchronized changes across multiple iterations. Through targeted activations of latent codes, Stable Artist can produce consistent results, reducing the need for prompt fine-tuning. Furthermore, it enables concurrent edits, allowing artists to capture the evolution of images and creating the illusion of the artist being autonomous. Notably, since the stable components are optimized to match semantic targets, they can be used to explain the image's semantic content. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics. High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is indeed a metric if $\alpha$ lies within the interval from $0$ to $0.5$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $1/(1-\alpha)$. The verification of this outcome was successfully demonstrated in the Lean proof assistant. Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. To make the most of this approach, we adopt an unconventional framework incorporating a sequential process of blur removal and subsequent reblurring with the assistance of a module that mimics real-world blur, as well as hand-crafted prior information based on advanced statistical human body models. This module not only enhances the deblurring algorithm's ability to distinguish between human and non-human regions but also improves overall outcomes compared to other recent state-of-the-art methods through adversarial learning. Experimental results show that our method outperforms other top methods with improved clarity and detail, particularly in image sequences that were previously unknown during training. A demo video of the method can be found at https://youtu.be/UL6 OsR9R8. The source code of this method is available at https://github.com/IndigoSky/HSD.

However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches utilize select, representative datasets, but this limited method restricts extensive analysis and introduces bias towards models that perform well on those chosen datasets, thus overlooking each dataset's distinct features. In response to these challenges, we aim to establish a new framework that integrates dataset profiling into the model selection process, providing more accurate model assessments. To justify this need, we address two critical questions: do scientific datasets have the potential to alter the ranking of competing models relative to traditional, generalized datasets, and could optimized, resource-efficient model evaluation enhance benchmarking reliability. Ultimately, the answers to these inquiries will establish a new foundation for a more effective and dataset-informed benchmarking strategy. Experimental findings on diverse datasets reveal that various models can be misrepresented by traditional benchmarks, demonstrating the need for dataset-specific profiling, while cost-efficient model evaluation using randomized sampling effectively evaluates models on large datasets, thereby creating opportunities for improved benchmarking methods.
